speechtext:
Mr. Speaker in the past I have indicated my pleasure in taking part in the debates of this House. However, this is a debate quite unlike any of the others. Nothing else we will ever debate here could be as grave or as serious as that which now concerns us, namely, the issue of capital punishment. The things which I intend to say today will, for me, be among the most difficult things I shall ever say at any time; but I feel they must be said. Unlike some previous occasions, however, it will not be particularly pleasurable to stand here today and argue against the government's Bill C-84 and in favour of capital punishment. I, very deeply and sincerely, believe that capital punishment should be part of any just system of law, and today I will try to explain some of the reasons I am a retentionist and why I believe as I do.
I know it is intellectually unfashionable to be a retentionist. The feeling that sometimes capital punishment- execution-is the only right and just way to deal with certain criminals bothers intellectuals. This feeling does not fit neatly into their computers and it is not compatible with their flow charts, diagrams and neat tables of statistics. The irrational actions of a murderer who goes on a rampage and slaughters innocent people greatly upsets the ordered and logical world of these intellectuals. Well, Mr. Speaker, I certainly have never claimed to be an intellectual, but maybe someone like myself is closer to the thinking and feeling of many ordinary Canadians than are all the intellectuals.

May 11, 1976
Capital Punishment
The argument of those who are against capital punishment is that it does not prevent murder. I do not think this can be either proved or disproved. The abolitionists claim that a comparison of states with capital punishment to those without shows no difference in the murder rate. The trouble with these comparisons, Mr. Speaker, is that they really are not comparisons at all, because they all involve countries of the western world. The fact is that no country in the western world today actually practices capital punishment. Some have abolished it in law, and some have not; but in practice, all countries of the western world-with the possible exception of some states in Africa-are abolitionist. Surely we are not so naive that we do not think murderers are aware of this fact. James O. Wilson, a professor of government at Harvard University, writing in the New York Times Magazine on October 28, 1973, stated:
There is no way of knowing what the effect of capital punishment would have been in the last decade or two if more convicted murderers had in fact paid the death penalty.
I am suspicious of statistics because I do not think they necessarily prove anything one way or another. However, having said that, and exercising appropriate caution, a look at the murder rate and the attempted murder rate in Canada during the last 20 years or so is very revealing. Statistics Canada figures indicate that in 1955 the murder rate in Canada, per 100,000 population, was .9. That is slightly less than one person per every 100,000. Six years later, in 1961, it had risen to 1.2 per 100,000. By 1967 it had risen to 1.8 per 100,000. The increase in the six-year period from 1961 to 1967 was exactly double that of the increase in the previous six-year period from 1955 to 1961.
This rate of increase was maintained, and increased slightly during the next seven-year period. In 1974, according to Statistics Canada, the murder rate per 100,000 population was 2.6. The actual number of murders committed in Canada in each of these years was: in 1955, 118; in 1961, 185; in 1967, 282; in 1974, 539. In other words, during about a 20-year period the number of murders committed in Canada showed almost a fivefold increase.
The figures for attempted murders in Canada are even more startling. For instance, in 1961 there were 74 attempted murders in Canada, a ratio of .5 per 100,000 population. In 1967 there were 139 attempted murders, a ratio of .9 per 100,000 population. In 1974 there were 524 attempted murders, a ratio of 2.3. So in a 13-year period from 1961 to 1974, the actual number of attempted murders in Canada increased almost eight times. It is interesting, I think, that this increase should take place almost exactly during the period following the point when capital punishment in Canada was abolished-in fact, if not in law, the year 1962, the last year anyone was executed in Canada.
I am not trying to suggest, by these figures, Mr. Speaker, that if we had had capital punishment during the last 15 years the murder rate and the attempted murder rate would have been any lower. It may have been; I do not know. No one can prove that it would have been, one way or another. But is it not just possible that it is more than merely coincidence that the number of murders and attempted murders in Canada showed such an increase during that period when capital punishment was not in effect, which has been characterized, as well, by increas-

ingly more relaxed moral values and more and more permissive attitudes toward human behaviour?
Is there really any difference between the attitude of those criminologists and penologists who believe that massive expenditures of money and resources can reform the most incorrigible murderer, and the attitude of those progressive educationalists who believe that children should be allowed to "do their own thing" in our schools and that any sort of order or discipline might stunt their creative growth? Who can deny that violent and bloody crimes among our adult population, vandalism in our schools and delinquency among our children has increased tremendously in the last 15 years? Are we so naive that we believe adult criminal and juvenile delinquents are not aware of the permissiveness of our society and the soft way it handles wrongdoers?
A Canadian Press story out of Toronto this past winter, which was carried by the Winnipeg Free Press on March 18, told of a metropolitan Toronto policeman, staff sergeant Jack Foster, who resigned just two years short of the 30 which he needed for a pension because of the anger and frustration which he felt after watching what was happening in the courts every day. He felt that he just could not remain a policeman and continue to observe it any longer. To quote Sergeant Foster:
As far as I am concerned, what is happening in the courts is a joke, just like a circus sideshow. The young people coming before the courts are treating the whole thing as a joke. They leave there laughing.
Mr. Speaker, maybe I am old-fashioned, but I do believe that there are moral absolutes, that there are things which are right and things which are wrong. There are still behaviours which a moral and just society must find unacceptable, and those who wrongfully and wilfully commit these actions are criminals and must be treated as such. Of course, this is today a very unfashionable attitude. The concept of evil as an absolute has gone out of fashion, the same as has the concept of absolute virtue. There are no saints today, and there are no sinners either. We must be the first society in history not to recognize or want to recognize that there can be bad and evil in men. Criminals today are not bad at all: they are just misunderstood, misguided, underprivileged and unloved! Well, Mr. Speaker, I may be old-fashioned, as I said, but I think some criminals are not any of these things at all. I think they are greedy, selfish, unscrupulous, evil and incredibly dangerous to a peaceful society.
A popular movie a few years ago involved a hunt for a criminal whose particular practice was kidnapping and then killing his hostage. This had happened on three or four separate occasions and the police had not been able to apprehend him. The hero of the picture voiced the opinion that the killer would likely do the same thing again within the next 24 hours, that there would be another kidnapping and possibly another murder by the killer. The chief of police asked the hero why he thought so, to which the hero replied, "Because he likes it."
Mr. Speaker, the crime of kidnapping and then threatening or killing the hostage has become very familiar to us in Canada during the last few years. So have other hideous and violent crimes. Canadians have become sickened by crimes involving the multiple slaying of young children, crimes involving rape, mutilation and torture killing of the
May 11, 1976

victims, and crimes in which the victims have been killed just for sport, having been robbed. What is an acceptable way of dealing with these criminals, this type of cancer in our society? Can it be treated any more than much of the cancer of the human body can be treated? Surely we must recognize and accept that at some point the only acceptable way of dealing with some criminals is by cutting them out of society in the way cancer is cut out of the body-by eliminating them, by execution. To me, the issue of capital punishment is essentially one of justice.
First, what is justice and how do we define it? We begin by making a distinction between what is right and what is wrong. A determination of what is right and what is wrong begins with a concept of what is fair. We set up a system of laws in an attempt to provide a reasonable degree of fairness to all members of society. When we set up laws, we must also attach to them a system of penalties for breaking them. This is the only way that the law can be made to work. If there is no penalty for breaking the law, then it is not enforced and it is not a law at all but merely a suggestion or good advice. The law must be enforced if justice is to prevail. Penalties for breaking the law are an affirmation of our belief in the rule of law and of our desire to see that justice is done.
The rule of law, then, requires, to be effective, that when a law is broken and a crime is committed, a penalty must be imposed. A retentionist believes that the penalty for murder must be execution. The abolitionists are troubled by the fact that capital punishment as a penalty for a crime involves killing, and therefore seems contrary to the supreme commandment against killings, and itself contradictory. But, surely, this view is a distortion of both justice and the true meaning of the commandments. Murder is a crime, but so is stealing or kidnapping in our society. How do we deal with them? We imprison kidnappers and impose fines for certain offences involving theft. Does anyone question that this is a fair and just way of dealing with these crimes? We do not classify these penalties as kidnapping and robbery by the state. They are the necessary penalties if the rule of law is to be maintained and justice is to be done. So it is with capital punishment.
One of the things which distinguishes a civilized society from anarchy is that it operates according to the rule of law. The basic tenet of this rule of law in any civilized society is that the most important and precious thing which an individual can possess is his life and that society will act to protect his right to life. The ultimate transgression of this law is for one member of society to deprive another member of his life, to commit murder. It is the murderer who makes the choice. By his act of murder he has chosen to remove himself from that society of which he was a part, to remove himself from its civilization and its humanity. His act of murder has forfeited his membership in that society. It then becomes the necessary duty of society to pronounce upon the ultimate transgression of its own laws by one of its members, if the society has any meaning at all and membership in it has any value. The killer brutalizes by his actions. He indicates that he has become less than that which society demands of him. The convicted killer has, by his actions, proven himself
Capital Punishment
unworthy to be part of a society which believes, above all else, in the sanctity of human life.
Some abolitionists are opposed to capital punishment because to them it seems like nothing more than a vengeful and barbaric "eye for an eye and tooth for a tooth" type of justice. It is nothing of the sort. It is merely an attempt to make the punishment the equivalent of the crime. The penalty must be equal to the offence or else it fails to be fair an just. The symbolic representation of justice is that of a blindfolded woman holding a sword in one hand and scales in the other. The blindfold represents the impartiality of justice, and the scales indicate that justice must be even-handed, with the award or penalty equal to the offence.
What is the right and the just way to treat some of the murderous criminals who confront us today? What is justice for a mass slayer of children, an airplane saboteur whose actions are directly responsible for the hideous death of perhaps hundreds of people, a sadist who tortures to death his victims, a robber who purposelessly kills his victims? Is imprisonment really justice for these criminals? Their victims cry out for justice, and we fail them. We reject the justice of the ancients as primitive and brutal. We want to be modern and sophisticated in our approach to crime, but in so doing we fail terribly in respect of justice. The result is that our society today is more brutal and primitive than anything imagined by the ancients.
Among ordinary people there is, today, a mood of anxiety and quiet desperation as they observe and are aware of a justice system which cares more for the welfare of the criminal than it does for that of the victims. Thousands of dollars are spent to maintain and keep the criminals, and nothing is done for their widows and victims. Do we not think that the ordinary person, is aware of this? He feels betrayed and acts to try to defend and avenge himself.
In our big cities, taxi drivers are held up and robbed with increasing regularity. In United States cities, taxi drivers carry guns under the front seat. I do not know if any in Canada do yet, but how long will it be before they start doing so? Storekeepers install elaborate burglary systems in their stores. The attendants at all-night gasoline stations sit in bullet-proof glass booths and do not carry any change after regular hours. I understand that in the city of Detroit the attendants even wear revolvers in an attempt to prevent hold-ups. Bus drivers are forbidden to sell tickets so that they will not have to carry any money and thereby invite robbery. Women take courses in selfdefence because they despair of receiving justice before the courts of law if they survive an attack. Yet we have criminology experts like Dr. Fattah of Simon Fraser University who have the gall and effrontery to lecture Canadians and tell us that we do not have the right attitudes towards criminals.
The abolitionists argue that capital punishment is cruel and unmerciful. They do not feel that any murderer should be executed. But mercy cannot be considered in isolation from truth and justice. To commute the death sentence for one murderer may be extending deserved mercy, but to extend this type of mercy to all thugs and murderers is to throw pearls before swine. We are moral beings accountable for our actions. If we dispense forgiveness and mercy

May 11, 1976
Capital Punishment
in wholesale lots to those who have not earned it by repentance, then we cheapen both mercy and justice. We offend God's law, rather than act in accordance with it. The Bible teaches us that God is a merciful God, but it teaches us that he is first of all a just God. The Bible has a lot to say about life, mercy and forgiveness, but it never questions the essential justice of execution for murder. Again and again it reiterates what the consequences of murder are: "He that smiteth a man, so that he die, shall be surely put to death". Also, "and they that take the sword, shall perish with the sword"; "whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed". In Acts 25:11, the Apostle Paul said:
If then I am a criminal, and have committed anything for which I deserve to die, I do not beg off and seek to escape death.
What the ancient societies knew and accepted, today we doubt and deny, and in so doing we have abdicated justice. Capital punishment is horrible, of course it is, and who can deny it. But is not the nature of all punishment horrible? No penalty can be both sophisticated and effective at the same time, but that does not make it any less necessary or just. To abolish it is to sacrifice the element of justice inherent in it, to be weak when we should be strong, to lack the courage that is required by our convictions of what is just and right.

I thank hon. members for their courtesy. I have only a few more comments to make. We live in a society which operates on the rule of law, as I have stated, and one of the basic tenets of both God's law and man's law is that human life is precious and important, the most precious of all human possessions. What is just penalty for the murderer who kills another, who deprives another being of his life, if not the forfeiture of his own? To require any less is to say that we do not really believe in justice, nor do we really believe that life is all that precious. Capital punishment for murder affirms our belief in justice and declares, in unequivocal terms, how important we regard life when we require that one who deprives another person of his life should thereby forfeit his own right to live.
We either live in a society where justice prevails, or we live in a society which without justice is not worth living in at all, because if there is no justice then life has no meaning. We either believe in the value of human life and are willing to affirm that belief by executing murderers, or we indicate, by failing to affirm this belief by not executing murderers, that life is both valueless and meaningless.
I choose to live in a society in which justice does prevail and in which life does have meaning. I desire a society which has the courage to affirm its belief in justice and the

importance of human life, and therefore I am unable to support this abolitionist, government bill.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday when I rose at this time on a point of order you indicated that you would take the matter under advisement. I gave notice at that time that I would rise today to amplify and complete my argument to attempt to illustrate that we are not following the intent of the Standing Orders of this House or that, at best, those Standing Orders are being misinterpreted. Let me say at the outset that my point of order is in no way intended to reflect on the subject matter of today's private members' hour or, for that matter, on the subject matter selected for any previous private members' hour. The point of order refers to the treatment or disposal of the bills or orders which precede on the order paper the item which is called for debate.

With reference to the remarks of the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Blais) yesterday, the suggestion was that this was the first complaint and that prior to making my comments I should have advised him. For his benefit, may I say that I have risen several times during this session on the same subject. Earlier in the session he will read on the order paper that an item of private members' business was, by unanimous consent, allowed to stand and retain its position. Resulting from my interventions at that time, the wording on the order paper has been changed. In addition, a sheet is distributed to hon. members indicating the business which is likely to be called in private members' hours. The sheet generally arrives late in the week after one or two private members' hours have passed. The sheet is not available to the public, which might be taking an interest in House business.
For this point of order today I can use almost any recent private members' hour, but for emphasis I will use the particular day which best illustrates the ridiculous position into which we are putting ourselves, the thirteenth day of last month. On that day the item called was No. 112 on the list of public bills. It is interesting to note that this particular bill was preceded by public bills sponsored by 28 different hon. members of this House. Several of those hon. members has more than one bill on the list.
The hon. member who is moving the bill listed for debate today has a total of ten bills listed prior to the one which was called for debate. The hon. member who moved his public bill that day himself had four other bills listed before the one which was called. All these bills, including those of the hon. member who spoke that day, retained their position on the order paper. Yesterday the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid), an acknowledged expert on House procedures, said:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to say that I do not believe the government should have the right to dictate what takes place in private members' hours. That is the right of the private member. If private members choose not to have their business come forward, that is their right. I do not believe the government should impose on the House of Commons what is to be taken up in private members' hours-
If I may-as everyone else does-I will quote an extract from Beauchesne's. I am quoting from citation No. 87 which reads as follows:
When an order of the day has been read, it must thereupon be proceeded with, appointed for a future day, or discharged.
Mr. Speaker, on April 25 of last year, if I may quote Your Honour, you said the following:
The hon. member has the right to raise this point of order again. I should like to refer him to standing Order 18( 1) which reads:
"All items standing on the orders of the day, except government
orders, shall be taken up according to the precedence assigned to each
on the order paper."
By the rule books this means that the House should call item by item those that appear on the order paper. The only problem is that if they are not proceeded with they go down to the end of the list, and the hon. member directly concerned loses his turn.
If the hon. member does not give unanimous consent I will call each of the bills on the order paper, one by one.
I suggest that if we had followed that procedure on April 25, 1975, we would have run out of time before the debate had started on the particular bill in question. I have one

An indication of consent or otherwise from the government as to the ability of a bill or any other measure to stand and retain its priority is no different from the indication of any other member of the House.
The point I am trying to make-and I find it somewhat difficult; I have to rise many times-is that we must have some prior knowledge of the business which is to be conducted in this House. Under the present procedures, this is an impossibility. It is not only difficult for hon. members, but it is an impossibility for the public, and I think the public is certainly entitled to know what is to be going on in this House in the way of business. The business should be listed on the order paper. We should know what is coming up. That is the precedent which was established in the past.
In view of these additional arguments, Your Honour may wish to take this whole matter under advisement and give a ruling later. Private Members' Public Bills
can be disposed of in any given session. At the beginning of each session a lot is drawn; a number of bills are drawn out. So when we dispose of 30 items of private members' business in a session, we do very well. Individual members who have had the luck of the draw want to preserve their priority. It was in order to accommodate them that we adopted the procedure we are now following.
Under Standing Order 19 there is provision whereby any order that is called, and with which the hon. member is not ready to proceed for one reason or another, can be stood at the request of the government. That is stipulated by the Standing Order. That was brought into being because of the hon. member for Vaudreuil bringing to the attention of the House basically the point he is making now. Evidently, all members opposite do not share his views. There was an indication by hon. members generally, however, that the procedure which was accepted by the House-namely, that the government express this wish through the parliamentary secretary to have all matters stood-was acceptable to individual members. That is the extent of government intervention; it lends its name to private members who do not wish to have matters debated at the time they are called, but by the same token do not wish to lose their priority. Effectively, we accommodate private members by proceeding in this way.
The hon. member for Vaudreuil has drawn our attention to a situation in which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) was involved when we dealt with Bill C-311 although there were a number of bills preceding it. I agree that in that one instance in the session we abandoned the usual course, which is to review all items in their order of priority, by asking all individuals in that priority whether they wanted their business proceeded with.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre had Bills C-250, C-256, C-260 and C-288 on the list ahead of Bill C-311. He did not wish to proceed with those matters, and we approached him to give him the time that was available because he had precedence. He inquired whether we could deal with Bill C-311. The matter was discussed and I used my discretion-and perhaps I am being attacked now for having done so-in according to a very honourable member of the House the privilege of dealing with an item which, in effect, was not in accordance with the usual procedures that we follow. The matter was disposed of in due course. Was I wrong in exercision that discretion? If I was, I stand to be judged.
All I want to indicate, Mr. Speaker, is that we attempt to provide to hon. members as soon as practicable those items which will be dealt with in the next session, first contacting the individual members who have priority in order to determine whether they will be available and whether they wish to proceed with a particular item of business. Having ensured that a member will be here to debate the item of business, we communicate with the interested parties, including the government. Then we set the matter down and advise all hon. members of the matter that is going to be debated on a given day.
There is a limitation on the amount of time available in which to advise members and the public generally, because of the allocation of government supply days. As you know, Mr. Speaker, a certain number of days are designated for

the opposition but they are not determined so far in advance that we know exactly when they will come. Private members' bills, of course, cannot be dealt with on those days. It becomes very difficult for us to advise members what business will be dealt with in private members' hour unless we know when opposition days will be set. Effectively, that puts certain restraints upon us. So we have two very serious limitations as far as giving prior notice. One is ascertaining that private members are ready to proceed, and the other is ascertaining when there is going to be a private members' hour.
Those are my submissions, Mr. Speaker. I think the whole matter can be resolved by the proper application of Standing Order 19(1) which reads as follows:
Questions put by members and notices of motions, not taken up when called may (upon the request of the government) be allowed to stand and retain their precedence; otherwise they will disappear from the order paper. They may, however, be renewed.
What the government has been doing is giving its consent in accordance with Standing Order 19(1).

Mr. Speaker, there is just one facet of this matter on which I should like to say a word or two, and I had intended to do that before I was dragged into this debate by the references from across the floor. May I simply say, with respect to that bill of mine far down the list that was allowed on April 13, that the information communicated to me at that time was that nobody with a bill ahead of mine was prepared to go, and I was. I also point out that on two occasions when I was allowed time for that bill, I surrendered it. On one occasion it was so that we could deal with the prisoner of war legislation, and on another occasion it was so that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) could make his statement with respect to the patriation of the British North America Act.
The one point about which I should like to say a word is that raised by the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) and also by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid) the other day; that is, the use of the phrase which appears in the order paper repeatedly, "allowed to stand at the request of the government". The Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Blais) has pointed out quite clearly that this is just a device. Actually, what happens is that the member requests that his bill stand, but since the rule book says it has to be done at the request of the government, he asks the government to do it. The government makes the request, and the matter stands.
I join with the parliamentary secretary in welcoming the fact that this whole matter is in the hands of a subcommittee of the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization. I hope this aspect of it will be sorted out so that we do not use this phrase which means something other than what we really mean. What happens is that a member requests that his bill stands, but it appears in the record as though the government requested it, and that enables the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River to say that somehow the government is interfering with private members' business.
If I may recall those ancient days when I first came here, the rule was a little different. In those days a matter could stand once, but the second time it was called-and I think
May 11, 1976

the hon. member for Vaudreuil might like this proposal-it was dropped unless there was unanimous consent for it to stay on the order paper. The change from that practice, that is, to having the government request it, was to get around the fact that sometimes some mean persons would not give their consent. I want to express the hope that a way can be found so that in reasonable cases bills can be allowed to stand; but it should be made clear that this has been done at the request of the member himself, so that it does not seem as if the government has the entire say about the matter.

Mr. Speaker, the last two interventions require some comment. If I may answer the comments of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre concerning the members who preceded him on the particular day in question, I point out-this is not in any way meant to be personal-that I had three bills which preceded the particular bill called, and considered each of them important enough to bring before the House if given the opportunity. I mention this only as I assume that several of the other 28 members may be in the same position.
But I was told nobody else was ready.

That is correct. The subject raised that day was the same subject being discussed on the floor of the House under government orders. In other words, I assume it would have been possible for the hon. member to raise his matter in the form of an amendment to the government bill actually under discussion that day, a bill to do with the Citizenship Act. The point is that many of us were most interested in the subject and would have welcomed, if we had known about it, the opportunity to participate in the private member's debate that day.
May I deal with the comments of the parliamentary secretary who referred to Standing Order 19(1). That part of the Standing Order which he quoted says, "Questions put by members and notices of motions . . ." He did not read the words "public bills." That point was referred to by the Acting Speaker on April 14, as reported in Hansard. As I have already pointed out, after the intervention of April 14 by the Acting Speaker, and that of April 25 by Mr. Deputy Speaker-yourself, sir-Mr. Speaker himself made a ruling on May 2. In the circumstances, I do not think we should heed the argument of the parliamentary secretary with regard to Standing Order 19.

Seriously, should the hon. member not consider the provisions of Standing Order 19(2) which reads in part:
Orders not proceeded with when called, upon the like request, may be allowed to stand . ..
The difficulty, it seems to me, is that Standing Order 19(2) puts bills in the same category as questions and notices of motions.

Mr. Speaker, the parliamentary secretary read, and I quoted, part of Standing Order 19(1). I refer hon. members to the proceedings of April 14 during which there was reference to the whole of Standing Order 19.
Private Members' Public Bills
Despite what was said, Mr. Speaker ruled as he did on May
2.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. I thank hon. members for their contributions. I am not sure what kind of conclusion will flow from the matter I am about to bring to the attention of the House at this time.
The point the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) raised seems to be based on his contention that the House is not following the intent of the Standing Order, or is incorrectly interpreting Standing .Orders 18 and 19 to which he referred. To prove his point, the hon. member referred particularly to what happened on April 13 last when the House considered item 112 under public bills. He brought to the attention of the House the fact that the hon. member who had moved, as sponsor, the public bill that day himself had three or four other bills listed on the order paper which preceded the one called and were stood at the request of the government.
He also, in my opinion, referred to an occasion on which the House proceeded by unanimous consent. I am not sure if he meant that day, April 13, or another day. In any case, I remember one occasion when the hon. member raised the question but did not thereby really further his argument. He complained about the procedure being followed but gave the Chair the impression that he was ready to let the House proceed without forcing the Chair to make a decision.
Today the hon. member referred to citation 87, page 81, of Beauchesne's fourth edition. The last sentence of citation 87(1) reads:
When an order of the day has been read, it must thereupon be proceeded with, appointed for a future day, or discharged.
To support his argument, the hon. member contends that hon. members ought to know in advance the order of business and that even the public should have prior knowledge of the business of the House of Commons, if I may use his own words. I say to the hon. member that the Chair can only interpret the existing Standing Order even though the Chair may approve the principle he is putting forward. The Chair must first look at the standing order and then decide if the practices of the past conform with the Standing Order. I think Standing Order 18(1) and all of Standing Order 19 ought to be read into the record so that they can readily be referred to if a decision must be made later.
Standing Order 18(1) reads:
All items standing on the orders of the day, except government orders, shall be taken up according to the precedence assigned to each on the order paper.
Standing Order 19(1) reads:
Questions put by members and notices of motions, not taken up when called may (upon the request of the government) be allowed to stand and retain their precedence; otherwise they will disappear from the order paper. They may, however, be renewed.
Standing Order 19(2) reads:
Orders not proceeded with when called, upon the like request, may be allowed to stand retaining their precedence; otherwise they shall be dropped and be placed on the order paper for the next sitting after those of the same class at a similar stage.
The hon. member at this time asks the Chair to determine if the government is entitled, without consulting all hon. members of the House, to interfere as it wishes with
13412

May 11, 1976
Private Members' Public Bills
the order of House business during private members' hour. In my opinion, the difficulty stems from the words "All items . . . taken up according to . . The hon. member suggests that all items except government orders, should be considered according to precedence, or as they are listed on the order paper. On this, I suppose, all hon. members agree. But the main question is whether the government has power to request, without consulting hon. members, that an order shall be stood. Having read Standing Order 19(2), I conclude that the only person-or the only institution, if you like-which has the right to request that an order shall stand is the government.
In my opinion the Standing Order, it must have been put there for the same reason put forward by the parliamentary secretary. He suggested that it is the responsibility of the House leader to try to plan the work of the House for days in advance. He must give notice to other hon. members as to what day there will be a private members' hour or what order of the day will be taken.
The hon. member is asking the Chair to solve a problem that exists between the hon. member or other hon. members and the government or members of the House of Commons.
The Standing Order allows an order of the House to be stood at the request of the government. Only the government can make that request, but it is for the House to decide. Therefore the question is in what.way the House should decide. This is the difficulty I have to resolve. Possibly this point should be taken under advisement.
If I decided to apply Standing Order 19(2) strictly and forget about any agreement that might exist between the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Blais) or any other member of the government and other hon. members or parties as to the order of business for private members' hour, and forgot about the distribution of lists of private members' business which have been initiated in recent months, and in which the Chair is not involved, I should at this time call every order, one by one. If hon. members do not accept the request of the government to stand each of the orders, the Chair must decide whether that supersedes the right of the government. I would have to decide whether to put the question with regard to whether the order should be stood every time. This would involve valuable time being lost to private members' hour.
The suggestion was made by the parliamentary secretary, and even more strongly by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), that the whole matter be considered by the sub-committee on procedure and organization which has been formed to look into private members' business. That is a valid suggestion. I feel this is better than asking the Chair to make a decision on a Standing Order which is not clear as to the procedure of disposing of that difficulty, thus, how should the House refuse to stand any private member's item of business.
Without minimizing the right of the hon. member to express his point of view on the organization of private members' business and his right, and that of other members, to have more input into the order of business during private members' hour, I feel we should leave it at that. I

am still prepared to take the matter under advisement. However, I would prefer the sub-committee on procedure and organization to study the matter and possibly design a Standing Order that is more precise and satisfies hon. members of the House.
Agreed, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING REDEMPTION OF MORTGAGES
speechtext:
that Bill C-244, to amend the Interest Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I trust that there is enough time remaining in private members' hour for me to put on record some of the notes I have on this matter. I will not speak too long in order that my bill will have a chance of being sent to committee.
The purpose of Bill C-244, as spelled out in the explanatory note, is to enable a mortgagor to redeem a mortgage by paying the amount of principal and interest then due, plus three months further interest. In this way unscrupulous mortgagees will be deterred from introducing excessively severe penalty clauses in small print. This is the specific and narrow purpose of my bill, which in short would stop pre-payment penalties that range from three months interest and upward.
However, the broader and more important reason for going ahead with Bill C-244 this afternoon is to provide members with at least an hour-of course on this occasion we will not have that much time-or hopefully more time if hon. members should decide the bill or subject matter should be sent to committee, to discuss from the borrower's side some of the smaller aspects of mortgages which are often overlooked when discussing the fundamental problem of interest rates.
I am viewing this from the borrower's point of view, for which I make no apologies, Mr. Speaker. The large lenders-the banks, trust companies and insurance companies-have always had the resources and expertise to argue their case more than adequately. Indeed within the wide parameter of the law they have, to a large degree, been able to write many of the rules. These institutions have a large and powerful voice when arguing for changes which would be to their benefit, or against those to their detriment. Granted, financial institutions are in business to make profit, but the nature of the business, considering the security they demand, leaves them the minimum of risk, virtually in a "no loss position". If chartered banks and
May 11, 1976

other lending institutions were experiencing financial difficulties, one could be more sympathetic. However, this is not the case. On the contrary, their profits are almost embarrassingly high.
The borrower, for his part, is just one individual who has really little or no say about the conditions of the mortgage. Oh yes, he may shop around, but this assumes that there are some real differences between mortgages offered, which may or may not be the case; also, he must possess a good knowledge of mortgages, which most do not have, only about 15 to 20 per cent of the population do so, and he must have the financial resources to pick and choose. For many people they must accept any mortgage they can get.
If we look at the borrower as a consumer, which he is, he may very well be the least knowledgeable, have the most limited choice of options, be the poorest organized and, in short, have the weakest bargaining position of any consumer in the country, and all this in relation to a product which normally will be the largest and most important investment in an individual's lifetime.
The mortgage market field cannot be considered a free market system like others. Not only is the commodity just too important and basic, but the relative strength between the buyers and sellers is simply too one-sided in favour of the lenders. For this reason government must be more than just a neutral, non-biased umpire. It must play an active role in strengthening the hand of the borrower or, conversely, limiting the power of the lender. I feel the excessively high pre-payment penalties are one such area in which it should act.
In my mind the whole concept of penalties for pre-payment of mortgages is questionable, but I can see some justification in the case where mortgage rates have dropped significantly and the lender may have difficulty finding another mortgagor. There may be some justification in that sort of situation, but that is virtually the direct opposite of the prevalent mortgage market today.
Take a situation where John Doe obtained a five year term mortgage in 1973 for, let us say, a 9 per cent interest rate, and today his rich Aunt Sadie leaves him $50,000, or he wins some lottery or whatever. Anyway, he has enough money to pay off the principal and interest due on the mortgage, which he does. Now this is really going to break up the lender. Oh yes, Mr. Speakers, for tomorrow in all likelihood he will lend that money out again to someone else, not at 9 per cent but probably something closer to 12 per cent. And John Doe, for the dastardly deed he has done to the poor lender, must pay a penalty of "x" months interest. This is totally ridiculous. The lender should be the one who pays John Doe a bonus for this kind of pre-payment.
I want to make it clear that although my bill suggests a pre-payment penalty of three months interest, it is just that, a suggestion for a maximum penalty allowed. Indeed I would want to change the bill. Proposed section 10.1 provides:
Notwithstanding anything contained in this or any other Act, a mortgagor may, during the term of the mortgage, redeem the mortgage for the amount of principal and interest then due, plus three months further interest.
Interest Act
I wish to insert after the word "plus", the words "a maximum of".
I would like to see some flexibility built into this part of the act so that the penalties reflect as much as possible the current mortgage market conditions, including provisions for the payment of bonuses to borrowers when pre-payment is advantageous to the lender. The government must watch carefully to make sure that financial institutions do not use this kind of proposed toughening of the existing regulations and other as an excuse to divert funds from the mortgage field or to opt for shorter term mortgages.
Before concluding, Mr. Speaker, I would like to touch on one other area which is related to the discussion this afternoon, and that is hidden closing costs. Today many lawyers and real estate brokers will advise clients to set aside at least $1,000 to cover these extra fees and pre-paid charges. Anyone who has ever bought a house knows that a broad range of items can show up at the last minute, including such obscure things as loan origination fee, loan discount points, appraisal fee, mortgage insurance application fee, pre-paid interest, pre-paid mortgage insurance premium, closing fee, and so on and so on.
Due to a law which came into effect last year in the United States, American home buyers are no longer surprised-perhaps shocked would be a more appropriate word-by such hidden closing costs. The U S. Real Estate Settlement Costs Act requires that the buyer be told to the penny how much it will cost to close on a house, exactly what each payment is for, and even what the previous buyer paid for the house if he or she owned it for less than two years. In addition, buyers must be given at least 12 days before they sign the final papers to look over the disclosure forms. If they do not like what they see, they can cancel the deal.
In Canada no such similar legislation exists to help home buyers. While much of what is contained in the U.S. act falls under provincial jurisdiction, I believe the federal government has a certain obligation to try to encourage similar legislation in this country, especially since the real estate and the lending industries do not appear willing to make full disclosure on a voluntary basis.
I hope hon. members may find that these minor problems, minor only in the light of the enormous over-all problems of housing and mortgage rates, are worth a more detailed examination, and as such decide the bill or its subject matter be referred to the Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs Committee of the House of Commons.
I understand from the parliamentary secretary that it is suggested that the bill should not now be read the second time but that the order be discharged, the bill withdrawn, and the subject matter referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. I want to say that I agree with this disposition of my bill and that the subject matter be referred to the committee. It is far better that the subject matter be referred to the committee than that the bill be talked out.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING REDEMPTION OF MORTGAGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-244 is a step in the right direction but it really does not amount to very much. It is like a raindrop in a downpour. I should like through you, Mr. Speaker, to remind the hon. member that it was his government that set afoot the high increases
95568-15y2

May 11, 1976
Interest Act
in interest rates. In fact Canada has the highest interest rates in the world, the highest housing costs in the world, and highest land costs. This is the reputation that his government has earned over the years.
I recall that when we amended the Bank Act in 1967 we opened the floodgates in regard to high interest rates. At that time under the Bank Act there was a ceiling of 6 per cent, but we found that lending institutions, and more especially the banks, would not participate in the mortgage field. What they forced from the government was the taking off of that 6 per cent ceiling on interest rates, and from that time forward we have had ascending interest rates for loans, and more especially mortgage loans, across the country. This is the credit that can be attributed to the Liberal government.
I had just come here in 1965 and I recall how some of the younger members of the party opposite attempted to stop this removal of the ceiling. The Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) was one of those who joined Walter Gordon in trying to prevent the taking off of this ceiling, and many other young Liberals also made the same attempt. But the then minister of finance, the present House leader, persuaded them that if they took off the ceiling there would be competition in the business world and that the rates would stabilize, or even go down. That did not happen, and it was the first mistake that the Liberal government made in regard to interest rates.
The second step was when Paul Hellyer in 1969 persuaded the government that mortgages should not be written for 25 year terms but rather five year terms, so as to make adjustments of interest rates in accordance with current trends. This was the price that he had to pay to the financial institution in order to persuade them to put money into mortgages. The result has been that, at the end of every five years of a mortgage term, people experience an increase in their interest rates. Under the old mortgage system the term was 20 or 25 years and the mortgagor had the security of knowing that the interest rate applied for that time.
When the interest rate ceiling was taken off in 1967 there was attached to CMHC mortgages, which were also at a rate of 6 per cent, a formula setting the rate at one per cent or VA per cent above the yield on bonds. That gave some control. But Mr. Hellyer was not satisfied with that; he also took off that control. He took off controls with regard to CMHC mortgages, so the combined effect of taking off control on mortgage interest rates and reducing the term from 25 years to five years is, as I say, that we have a reputation in Canada of having the highest interest rates in the world, with the highest land costs, and the highest housing cost. That is why I say that what the hon. member is attempting to do amounts to very little in the big scene regarding interest rates.
I am going to put on record just what interest rates do in respect of housing. I have a few figures here that I carry around in my wallet, because when I speak on housing from time to time it is nice to have a few figures to quote. This is what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) also does with regard to pensions. He has always got information on pensions right in his pocket so

he will have ready reference to it. I do the same thing with regard to housing interest rates.
Let me give some figures regarding a mortgage for $25,000 for a term of 25 years at 11 per cent. The monthly payments will be $240.64, and over that 25-year period the borrower will pay $72,192. If that mortgage were at 6 per cent the borrower would pay $159.97 a month and the total amount would be $47,991, a difference of $25,000.
In today's market one knows that a $25,000 mortgage really will not finance a home, and that you have to get up to at least a $40,000 mortgage. On a $40,000 mortgage at 11 per cent a person pays $385.02 per month over a 25-year period, and the total amount that would be paid is $115,506. On a $40,000 mortgage at 6 per cent for 25 years the person pays $255.94 a month for a total of $76,782. In other words the difference between a $40,000 mortgage at 11 per cent and a $40,000 mortgage at 6 per cent over a 25-year term amounts to $39,000. That $39,000 is what the borrower has to pay in difference if he gets a mortgage at 11 per cent as compared to 6 per cent.
In biblical times they used to talk about usury. That is a word that was replete in the Old Testament. We should bring it back today. The word usury should be used many times just to underline to borrowers what is taking place.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING REDEMPTION OF MORTGAGES
speechtext: Maybe we should make it a capital offence.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING REDEMPTION OF MORTGAGES
speechtext:
The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) suggests that usury should be a capital offence, and I am inclined to agree with him.
This is the problem with which we are faced. The step the hon. member suggests is a step in the right direction, but it is a very small step toward solving the problem of high interest rates. I know the hon. member is one who is concerned about people. I have known him for a few years. He is a fellow lawyer and I think he is concerned about people. If we are concerned about people we have to be concerned about their housing problems. We have to build affordable houses, as the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) suggests. If we are to build affordable houses we must look at interest rates. We must have interest rates which give the borrower a fair chance to pay off his mortgage. The only way this can be done is by having low interest rates. It is up to the government to control interest rates with regard to housing so that people can afford them.
It is up to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs to bring forth legislation which controls financial institutions, banks, mortgage companies, trust companies, and insurance companies so they do not charge unconscionable and usurious interest rates.
In order that the bill is not talked out let me conclude by saying I am in favour of it but, my gracious, it is a very short step with respect to a big problem.
