subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no one will deny that the question of whether or not to abolish capital punishment is the most difficult problem likely to
Capital Punishment
be faced by members of this thirtieth parliament. Few, if any, other issues have attracted as much public attention and concern. Debate in the media has centred not only on whether the use of the death penalty should be ended, but also on how members of parliament should reach their decisions. My mail has also reflected the divergence of opinion which exists on this point, that is, whether a member of parliament should vote according to his conscience or according to the views of the majority of his constituents.
During my election campaign I made it very clear that I am against all forms of killing, whether it be abortion, euthanasia, capital punishment, or war. My opposition to these methods of ending life varies by degree in relation to each of them. For example, I am completely opposed to abortion and would never vote in favour of a freer abortion law, even to the extent that I would put my seat in this House on the line. At the other end of the scale, I would make no such commitment against wars. Although ideally I would like to see an end to war, I do not feel that man has progressed to the point where war is obsolete.
My views on capital punishment fall in between those two extremes. Even though my personal feelings are for abolition, I cannot give a satisfactory answer to the question of the hired killer. In this case capital punishment is not a deterrent. There is no hope for rehabilitation of the criminal, yet society must be protected. I will be able, therefore, to live with a decision either way that is, to retain or abolish the use of capital punishment.
Realizing that I had the responsibility to take a stand on the issue, I was faced with the problem of what that stand should be. I decided to ask my constituents. In support of taking that action, I would like to refer hon. members on both sides of the House to a resolution passed at the National Convention of the Liberal Party of Canada in November, 1975. It was resolved that:
Members of Parliament be encouraged to canvass their constituents' opinions on specific and general policies.
This being a free vote, I feel that we have been given an ideal opportunity to democratize the decision making process in this instance. Certainly it is not practical or proper to survey popular opinion on every question with which we must deal, but on a moral issue of this nature I feel such action is justified and, indeed, essential. The alienation of the electorate from the government is becoming increasingly evident.
Here we have a chance to let the people know that they are being listened to. I campaigned on this theme in 1974, and I still feel that as the representative of my constituents I am here primarily to help enact the legislation that they want. For that reason I circulated a questionnaire to all households in my riding in March of this year. Of the 30,000 delivered, I received 6,008 completed returns, an over 20 per cent response. Any member who has surveyed his constituents will realize that that represents a very satisfactory return, one of the largest known. It also represents a suitable percentage for making a statistically accurate analysis.
In the questionnaire I asked four questions. Taking into account the proposed peace and security measures of Bill C-83, the first question asked whether the respondent favoured the abolition of capital punishment. For the

May 11, 1976
Capital Punishment
record, Mr. Speaker, I would like to show that the response to this question, as for the others, remained essentially the same no matter what the questionnaire return level was.
With 3.98 per cent of the questionnaires returned, 73.3 per cent of respondents were opposed to abolition of capital punishment. At the 7.9 per cent level, 72.1 per cent were opposed; at 12.52 per cent, 71.0 per cent were opposed; at 16.93 per cent, 70.5 per cent were opposed; at 18.2 per cent, 70.5 per cent remained opposed, and at the 20.03 per cent level, the final tally, 70.7 per cent of respondents were opposed to abolition. That result shows a clear and overwhelming support for the use of the death penalty.
Question No. 2 asked the 70.7 per cent who answered the first question in favour of capital punishment whether they wanted the death penalty reserved only for murders of police and prison guards. In this instance 86 per cent replied that no, those involved in enforcing the law should not be singled out for special consideration.
My third question asked the same people, those who favour retaining capital punishment, whether the death penalty should be available for use against those persons convicted of first degree murder as it is defined in Bill C-83. Ninety-five per cent replied in favour of capital punishment for that group of murderers.
Finally, I asked if I, as a member of parliament, should vote according to my own conscience on this issue. Sixty-six per cent replied that no, I should not. Therefore while approximately one third of my constituents feel that I should vote according to my conscience, two-thirds, representing a significant majority, feel that I should not, but instead should represent the majority feeling of my riding. I will, therefore, respect the wishes of that majority and not vote according to conscience, but instead will vote against Bill C-84.
As I explained earlier, the capital punishment issue provided an excellent opportunity for the government to seek public support for changing the existing law. Moral issues such as the one we are presently debating arise infrequently. Also there will be a free vote. With this situation, and the fact that two thirds of my constituents feel that I should vote according to the majority opinion, I feel that the government is wrong in not seeking the views of the majority of Canadians, and acting accordingly. Sixty per cent of those people responding to my questionnaire added their comments on the issue, and one comment that was made time and time again was that my constituents were very grateful for the opportunity to have their opinions heard and considered.
Although the deterrent effect of capital punishment has been widely debated, the fact that so many people believe that it is a deterrent should be seriously considered. In the same way as the rule of law will be ineffective unless everyone in society has respect for the law, if most Canadians feel that capital punishment does serve as a deterrent, it would be reasonable to assume that the general acceptance of that principle would lead to its having an effect on the general population. I feel in this instance that the government missed a great opportunity to redress the feeling of alienation now felt by many citizens of this country.

The government should listen to the people on questions related to deeply held moral beliefs.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: The hon. member for LaSalle.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Not for LaSalle, Mr. Speaker, for Joliette.
Mr. Speaker, when you asked me to speak, as the member for LaSalle, I thought you meant that the riding of Joliette belongs to LaSalle.
Mr. Speaker, I am aware that we are discussing a basic issue for the future of society. I realize also that this legislation is one of the most serious we ever discussed in the House.
I want to be quite clear and specific in my comments, and I want to say also to those who do not share my opinion, that I deeply respect their views.
I remember having the opportunity to discuss this matter since I arrived in this House in 1968, and I also remember that the debates were very interesting. I wish to say that my decision is final and that I will vote against the bill before us.
The public at large and those who advocate the abolition of capital punishment are often tempted to blame society. In their opinion, society is responsible for everything. I suggest that we have our own responsibilities within society. But the public is concerned and all the attempts made by this government since 1968 have not brought about the security which they are entitled to expect.
I had the opportunity to listen to a few speeches on Bill C-84. I wish to draw the attention of the House on the speech made this afternoon by the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner). Of course, others have also made excellent points for or against capital punishment, but I believe that all members of this House would benefit from reading again and again the remarks made by the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe. Given his experience, of course, for which I have much respect, he was dealing with a matter which he knows very well. He was able to discuss this matter much better and in a much more enlightened way than I. His comments deserve all my congratulations and I think he destroyed one after the other the arguments put forward by the Solicitor General in introducing this legislation.
When dealing with capital punishment, some people say it is a barbaric method. One must think, nevertheless, of these businessmen, these restaurant owners, these pharmacists or these people who work in banks and who have been unhappily shot down by people who had decided to overlook the respect for somebody else's life to achieve their purposes. I would be inclined, Mr. Speaker, to blame the government for not abiding in the first place, by the legislation now before us.
Like all my colleagues, I know that when we last discussed this matter, we agreed to enforce the death penalty for the murder of prison guards and policemen. Such has not been the case, and I remember, Mr. Speaker. The present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), when he intro-
May 11, 1976

duced and supported that legislation, made no secret of the fact that he would never enforce the death penalty while he was Prime Minister. Recently, the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) made no bones about the possibility of his resignation if his bill was defeated.
Mr. Speaker, when we have a government whose leader says he will not enforce a legislation he tries to sell us, I find that indecent and dishonest. We had democratically voted in this House on a legislation which has not been applied. Of course, some will say that the act gives the cabinet the authority to commute death sentences. But the act also says that capital punishment will apply when a prison guard or a police officer is killed with premeditation, and that has not been done.
Mr. Speaker, I will be very outspoken, this is not a matter of deterrence. Of course, members on all sides have tried to determine whether the implementation of capital punishment had a deterrent effect. As far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, it is a matter of justice. Whenever I am reminded of this ever actual commandment "Thou shalt not kill", I would like to point out to the murderers that this commandment should first apply to them and that they should know that whenever they choose, in order to achieve their ends, to get rid of anybody who happens to be in their way they should expect this kind of punishment.
I do not feel I am any worse than anyone else, Mr. Speaker. As far as I am concerned, I think that this is a matter of justice, and in this world of ours, I think we can consider it this way. Of course, there are not only members in the House of Commons but there are people in this world who are most scrupulous when the death penalty is being discussed. Mr. Speaker, should the House decide in favour of the death penalty, those who, in order to achieve their ends, intend to get rid of someone, will think twice before doing so. When one is squeamish about capital punishment, that is soon forgotten in wartime. That question was raised by one of my colleagues here in this House. Nobody hesitates Mr. Speaker, when one's country is at war, to fight and slaughter countless innocents.
Neither the Solicitor General nor anybody else has ever raised the matter of the indirect participation of Canada in the Vietnam war. Very little mention was made of it, Mr. Speaker, yet, I think we might have asked ourselves that question. To what extent have we not participated indirectly in the slaughter of thousands of Vietnamese? But it was interesting for certain industries, Mr. Speaker. Those scruples we have about the bill before us, we did not have them at the time, and I cannot remember the Solicitor General having deplored the indirect participation of Canada in that war. When a severe penalty must, of course, be imposed on that inveterate criminal, on that habitual murderer, on the one who, in order to achieve his purpose, plans to take the life of someone else, then we have scrupules.
Today, Mr. Speaker, with criminologists and psychologists-because I imagine there are a number of them in the office of the Solicitor General-one is tempted to make us believe that there are possibilities of rehabilitation. One is tempted also to say in particular that that always depends on society.
Capital Punishment
I am one of those who believe that we must improve the social climate and that considering the economic difficulties we are experiencing, this is not likely to reduce the number of robberies. But, Mr. Speaker, that is a long way from making a business out of it and a source of income to live in this earthly world.
Of course we all wish to improve that social climate by different steps. And why would we accept to forgive so easily a minority of people who allow themselves anything while the great majority endures that social climate which is so difficult, tolerates, waits out and still hopes that the situation might improve so as to be able to live decently and thus get an adequate income to allow them to live decently.
There was talk about a free vote. There is no doubt that on this side of the House all my colleagues will vote quite freely and according to their conscience. I have difficulty, Mr. Speaker, accepting that the Prime Minister should have gone as far as saying at one point that he might consider tendering his resignation if Parliament voted in favour of capital punishment. I have just as much difficulty accepting that the Solicitor General responsible for this bill should infer that he could not accept that his bill should not be passed. And how far will hon. government members try to cooperate and support not necessarily the bill but the minister in charge or the Prime Minister? When reference is made to a free vote I must say I have doubts.
Earlier a colleague talked about a certain survey. The survey made by the Metro Toronto Police Association is significant and quite clear. There was a question: Should capital punishment be retained for murders of policemen or guards? If you limit yourself to those categories, the answers are for the most part negative. But when we are asking people whether the death penalty should be retained for any crime, any premeditated crime, 87 per cent of them answer yes.
A few years ago, when the last vote was taken on capital punishment, I conducted like other members, an inquiry in my riding and 88 per cent of my constituents said they were in favour of capital punishment. I did not ask for another poll recently, but, like many other members, I have received my fair share of submissions and comments. It is quite clear that Canadians are in favour of capital punishment for inveterate criminals and those who commit premeditated crimes. That is quite clear. There are some reservations in respect of some forms of crime. When a convicted criminal is involved, the public recommends the application of the death penalty. I also know, as a result of investigations, that the public would be in favour of a referendum on this matter. Not only the Solicitor General but also the government know full well that a referendum on the matter would be decisively in favour of the death penalty in the cases I mentioned a while ago.
We are offered an alternative: 25 years in jail. Mention is made of 15 years in prison, with the possibility of a parole. But it is hard at this point to trust the government proposing such legislation: difficult because of the experiences made with regard to paroles and other practices which the people, generally, did not look upon kindly. Those experiences did not bring, not by a long shot, what the governm-nent has hoped. By refusing to apply the act it asked us to

May 11, 1976
Capital Punishment
pass a few years ago it also prevents us from trusting it as it hoped. The arguments invoked this afternoon by the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner), who is well versed in the matter, demolished one by one the arguments presented by the Solicitor General (Mr. All-mand). If he wants to prove his sincerity, even ever so slightly, I believe he could make comments tomorrow that would be quite contrary to those he made on introducing the bill.
And so, with all the chances of evasion we know, in the case of this 25-year imprisonment penalty, we know very well that the criminal condemned to that term in prison will not hesitate to commit another crime to escape from it. What does 25 years more or less mean when he has been sentenced to 25 years? I do not think that such a proposal is acceptable. A miscarriage of justice has also been mentioned. Of course, I am not a lawyer. I am an average man but I have my views on the matter. And the Solicitor General pointed out more particularly that the poor had an handicap because they could not afford costly defence lawyers as the rich do and were discriminated against from the start.
This is perhaps the best solution. This Parliament could provide the poor with as good a defence as that obtained by the rich. I think it is important to provide the accused with a complete defence which without being perfect would be equal to the defence given to those who can afford the best lawyers. I think Parliament should be responsible for ensuring that any individual benefits from an adequate defence when he is accused of murder.
The member for Saint-Hyacinthe said this afternoon and I have every reason to believe him owing to his experience as a judge, and other lawyers in the House have also stated that the mechanisms of justice were altered, that we had reason to believe that a miscarriage of justice could no longer happen. But to the extent that there is the shadow of a doubt, the enforcement of the death penalty could not be recommend. I think that those comments are commendable. I therefore consider only the well prepared premeditated murder by the criminal who will do anything to achieve his ends, as I said, to remove all those who stand in his way. The same goes for criminals who do not hesitate to get rid of an embarrassing witness in a future trial. I think that we are under the obligation perhaps to be stern but also to be fair. Mr. Speaker, we are also told that hanging is a somewhat savage process. We could come forward with measures or suggestions for some changes in this regard. We could also do away with someone who constitutes a danger for society by administering a pill or giving an injection; let us adopt another method if the rope seems repulsive to some people. It is important to maintain and to resume implementation of the death penalty.
My friend from Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) in winding up his speech last night insisted that we should all let our minds dwell on life, not on death. I would like my mind to dwell on the life of the innocents victims who were killed by criminals, Mr. Speaker. And like him, I let my mind dwell on life, on the life of those innocent people who, at a certain point in time, because of our parole system or as the result of convicts escaping, have met with the fate we know because we did not apply what I think is
[Mr. La Salle.)
needed, and what I consider a measure of justice for the unscrupulous killer.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, I could quote statements and statistics for or against it. When we refer to the possibility that an innocent person may have been hanged, we refuse to add up the number of innocent people who have been killed by those who deserved the death penalty and managed to get away with it by all sorts of means, resumed their criminal activities and killed a number of innocent people. It might be difficult to find out exactly how many such innocent people there have been, but we know very well that if we did add them up, the number would greatly exceed the number of judicial mistakes. Once again, thanks to more modern procedures, judicial mistakes have become virtually impossible, and where the flimsiest shadow of a doubt does exist, we do not recommend the death penalty. And if this government or this Parliament were to give the underprivileged the same defence opportunities as are available to the rich people, I believe that we would eradicate all doubts concerning charges made against anyone.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to take up too much time, but I would like to say that, in view of the wishes of the majority, this bill is unacceptable if we look at the present situation and the increase in the crime rate throughout Canada. As I live close to metropolitan Montreal, I am aware of what is going on there, and I believe that the situation is serious, with certain reservations concerning these crimes. Several other members have dealt with facts and submitted evidence.
I do not want to repeat all these facts and statistics tonight because others have done so before me, but again, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that we would benefit from going over the speach delivered here by the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe (M. Wagner). He spoke objectively, realistically and from experience, and therefore, I believe that we would benefit from reading this speech so as to truly understand the need and the necessity to apply the death penalty without feeling any less compassion for certain types of criminals and without favoring any less the improvement of our social climate, which could, in itself, reduce the crime rate, and without remaining any less open towards the assistance that we can give these unfortunate people.
Mr. Speaker, in closing, I wishing that true justice may finally be implemented in Canada.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Once again, Mr. Speaker, the House has to study a question which has raised a lot of controversies all over the country, and this for many years. Of course, it is not very interesting to discuss whether we should take the lives of some of our fellow human beings. But a fact remains: each man and each woman has the right to live and when someone dares to threaten deliberately the life of another human being I sincerely think that we do not have to protect his or her life as he or she has not protected that of the other.
Our goal today is to attempt to study this thorny question so that we can make decisions worthy of our civilization. Besides, to my mind, I think that the search for answers, as far as the taking of the lives of some of our fellow human beings is concerned, should be done very
May 11, 1976

carefully and prudently before considering total abolition of the death penalty, especially at a time when so many horrible crimes are committed.
Mr. Speaker, to abolish the death penalty, as Bill C-84 proposes, is like abandoning the innocent between the hands of the guilty and telling them just this: Listen, murderers, go ahead, do as you please. The law prescribes that nobody can touch you; furthermore, it aims at protecting your lives at the expense of the lives of your victims.
Unfortunately, the bill we are now studying would abolish the death penalty for people convicted of murder and replace the death penalty with life imprisonment. We can also notice that the new arrangements for the application of the death penalty will vary depending whether they concern first degree or second degree murder. First degree murder covers, if I refer to the bill, planned and deliberate murders and contracted murders, that is to say hired killers; the murder of a police officer or that of a prison guard in the course of their duties; murder committed during the hijacking of an aircraft, a kidnapping or certain sexual offences, including rape and attempted rape. As for other murders, for example murders due to jealousy, they are considered second degree murders. Relating to the sentence, individuals of first degree murder will serve a 25 years prison term before being qualified, for the first time, to apply for parole. Whereas individuals convicted of second degree murder will not be qualified to apply for parole before they have served ten years of their sentence. However, in this latter case, the judge will be allowed to extend the minimum period to be served before the inmate can qualify for parole; in this respect, a maximum sentence of 25 years has been provided for in this legislation.
Mr. Speaker, on March 4, 1974, the following appeared in the newspaper Le Droit, and I quote:
Is the death penalty better than a life sentence. In this connection, Pat Devlin, a prisoner at the Joyeeville penitentiary in Ontario stated: "It is better to impose the death penalty than to imprison an individual for life. The life of a prisoner is a brutalizing experience which cannot be understand by those who have not lived it. Criminals will not be rehabilitated by shutting them up in donjons."
Needless to say, free societies have an unalterable principle that the effect of the law is the same for everyone. From my early childhood, my parents have instilled that law into me. Today, the Solicitor General of Canada in presenting that bill seems to forget that principle since he wants us to accept two categories of murders, as I mentioned a while ago: first, the murder of policemen and guards which could entail a 25-year sentence without parole and, second, the murder of the so-called average citizens which would entail a 10-year sentence without parole. Big deal!
Mr. Speaker, we know that it was this House which decided that capital punishment would be retained in our Criminal Code for premeditated murder of a policeman or a prison guard, and we know that since 1962 there has not been a single hanging in Canada. Then why do we find those provisions in the Criminal Code if not to use them? For my part, I do not see any difference between the well planned murder of a policeman or a bank manager, for instance, or of an ordinary citizen, because the life of any
Capital Punishment
citizen is worth that of a policeman or a prison guard, and we cannot have a law for the rich and another for the poor.
If we retain capital punishment, we must realize that life has no age and that it is valuable to everyone whatever his social rank. I agree with the reasoning of legislators that the policeman-and I know what I am talking about because I have been a policeman myself for several years- has an important part to play in the protection of society and that his role justifies particular attention and protection, but we must not forget that in principle we are all equal under the law.
So, Mr. Speaker, it is not difficult to point out that the Solicitor General made another mistake in proposing Bill C-84 because how can he distinguish between the murder of a policeman and that of an ordinary citizen? Who would dare say that the murderer of a bank manager should have serve only a 15 year sentence? Once again, this bill makes a law for the rich and another for the poor and that seems to me very unfair.
So I believe that most not all members of the House, except, of course, the Solicitor General who dared propose such a bill to the Canadian people, will agree that the murder of a policeman is not different from the murder of any other citizen or a bank manager as I just mentioned.
Will capital punishment be retained or abolished in Canada? That is the question dividing opinions at this time. Some want to retain it to give greater security to society, others want to abolish it because it contradicts somes passages taken from the Bible. I conducted an inquiry recently in my riding, not only among the people I have known for a number of years, but more precisely among the heads of family. As a matter of fact, those who are in favour of reinstating capital punishment represented almost 85 per cent of the whole population. I received more than 1,240 letters and out of that number, over 1,000 were in favour of capital punishment.
Therefore, as we can see, this poll shows how important the question is to the people in the light of the number of murders committed these last few years in the province of Quebec and everywhere else in our country.
As I was saying, some claim that the Bible is against capital punishment, but to them I say this: the authority we personify comes from God. Now, the fact remains that if we base ourselves on the principle that capital punishment is barbaric and unworthy of a civilized era, we automatically deny that divine mandate.
On the other hand, I want to say that I agree that, for the unbeliever, the death penalty is unworthy of man and barbaric because, according to him death leads to naught, but, for me, a believer, my opinion should be entirely different, death being to my mind the passage from one life to another.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the God from whom we hold our authority did say:
Thou shalt not kill.
But it would also be fair to add that that same God provided the death penalty for he who would violate the precept. For in Genesis, chapter 9, verse 6, one reads this:
13420

May 11, 1976
Capital Punishment
Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man.
All that they lead into captivity will be lead into captivity; all that they take the sword will perish with the sword.
And I could continue indefinitely, but I simply quote from the texts to make you understand that the Bible is not opposed to capital punishment. Surely, I understand very well that respect for life is not the prerogative of Christians: this principle is good for everyone. In any case, you will agree with me that the Christian principles are not the whim of one religion in particular. But for all these reasons, I consider that the federal government must reinstate capital punishment and that, when the proof is made that the murderer acted deliberately and knowingly, capital punishment must be applied. But I agree that it is sometimes difficult to prove the deliberate character of an act, as it depends on numerous factors, but when crimes are committed with premeditation, capital punishment must be applied.
Since capital punishment is not applied any more, murders are increasing. The criminals know very well that they risk much less. As a matter of fact, it is usually easy to see that lawyers often try to turn a charge of first degree murder into a charge of second degree murder or those who are guilty enjoy the leniency of the Cabinet.
Mr. Speaker, I sincerely think that anyone killing deliberately must pay with his life for a crime so serious that nobody on this earth has a right to make an attempt on the life of his neighbour; and he who does so should be prepared to risk his own life.
If this government manages to have capital punishment abolished once and for all in this country, as they hope, one only has to believe then that the right lies within the power of the individual, that justice favours the strong and that finally strength prevails over law. Before concluding, I would like to point out that we probably are directly responsible for the fact that murderers have become wild beasts. As a matter of fact, several became so after serving long jail sentences and specially after having remained locked up too long because of our egoism.
So these men were compelled to rebel and take the only means available to force society to take care of them. Man lives in a society where there is no perfection because of its institutions, its structure and inequalities which, in time and with the means used, finally make him different from what he was naturally or ideologically meant to be. The sick society in which we live dictates to him a mode of living in a community, it imposes its laws which are derived from general behaviour and at the same time forces on him its ideas which will eventually become means of action that he will avail himself of to voice his protests against society. Then when this man has become aware that he is a robot in this society, a creature as imperfect as society itself, a being quite different from what he intended to be, he cannot do anything concrete to change his situation without being liable to a sanction which will compel him to pay for his wrongdoings, to repair the damage he has done to society.
True, it is important to ask oneself what attitude should be adopted towards murderers. However before we come to this issue, should we not wonder why there are killers, assassins and thieves since it is obvious that one does not
turn into a murderer overnight. No, Mr. Speaker, this is caused by our society which advocates permissiveness, and laisser faire. In this respect I would like to quote a few passages from a recent article in La Presse signed Suzanne and Francois Desmarais. I quote:
The deep cause of the rising crime rate, particularly among young people, is the rejection of all moral values.
This generates violence, family break up, free love, the so called sexual "liberation" alcohol and drug addiction. All this has been fostered by the media and magazine industry and by the legislation itself.
And further, Mr. Speaker, it says:
And when they talk of government responsibility, we would say this is the area where it should assert itself primarily. True, we must protect ourselves against an immediate threat but we must also go to the root of the problem and try to bring about the reforms which are required. We let evil go unbridled and now we want to check it with arbitrary laws.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, with the bill that the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) presented to us, it is exactly what the government is trying to do. For, after having served their sentence, what will the murderers do? Prisons are full now and what does the federal government do in the way of practical rehabilitation?
What happens to inmates after their release from prison? What chance do they have to go back to the society in which we live, considering their court records follow them for the rest of their life? I know by experience as a former policeman, and I mentioned it at the beginning of my speech, that almost nothing is done in penitentiaries and prisons to give the inmates a new lease on life. On the contrary, very often a prisoner spends many months without talking to a social worker and if on top of that he is deserted by his wife, his children or, if you like, by his family, how do you expect, Mr. Speaker, this prisoner to fit easily into this society which, as I said, is very sick? I sincerely regret that such things may exist but after further reflection I understand very well the view of Pat Devlin, the inmate of Joyceville penitentiary in Ontario whom I mentioned a few minutes ago.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I wish to quote a letter from a Mr. S. C. B. Robinson from Gananoque, in Ontario, who summarizes quite well the reasons for which I am favourable to the retention of capital punishment. I quote:
The value of life is a basic lesson of character, of reason and good sense that should be taught at home, at church, at school and through a whole series of social contacts. And, as a last resort, the state should teach it to those who did not understand and commit premeditated murders. At that stage, we should underline in an understandable manner the value of life and express it in a comparison with the own life of the murderer. In other words, the value of the victim's life should be equal to that of the murderer.
Capital punishment is a repulsive idea but society becomes absurd when it allows a murderer to kill a civil servant, beat a child to death or to shoot innocent by standers knowing very well that he will not pay with his own life.
A good number of our politicians claim that capital punishment is so repulsive that they cannot be party to its implementation but they declare that it is not repulsive enough to have a deterrent effect on a potential murderer. This reasoning seems perfectly illogical. The threat of capital punishment for the potential killer should allow the society to regulate a situation where the victim is unable to defend himself. Any other solution is favourable to the criminal and consequently, our citizens are less protected than they should be.
Capital punishment should not be applied to those who are convicted on circumstancial evidence and hanging should not necessarily be the only means to implement it but our nation should stop the present

May 11, 1976

inflation in the value of the murderer's life at the expense of that of the victim-we should be all equal before the law and before the murderer.
So, Mr. Speaker, for all those reasons, I think that the retention of capital punishment in Canada is the only means to ensure real justice to persons convicted of capital murder. So I wish that every member in this House before making a decision having serious effects on our society will prevail himself of the stronger arguments and forget once and for all the sentimentality as the future of our children, of our wives and of our fellow citizens depends on it.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on most occasions in this House members stand up and say how glad they are to speak on certain issues, but I think this is not a very happy occasion.
I should like to commence my remarks with a quote from W. Gunther Plaut, a rabbi from the Holy Blossom Temple in Toronto:
At this late stage what new light can anyone shed on the controversy over capital punishment? After all the arguments on both sides have been made with passion and the full force of reasoned argument-one must come to the conclusion that even if the debate continues from now until doomsday no one will get any wiser. For truth be told: wisdom is not at all involved in the decision.
With these opening remarks, Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out to the House and the people of Canada the archaic way we govern ourselves in this House at the present time, and the great need for reform. I am quite convinced, as I am sure are the people of Canada, that most members-by most I mean all but 2 to 3 per cent of the members sitting in this House-have decided which way they are going to vote, be it through emotion, through their hearts, or through the direction of their constituents.
This has been an emotional issue in this whole scenario in the House ever since 1962. We have stood up here as supposedly the champions of the people of Canada. We have emotionally involved not only ourselves but the people of Canada in a conflict, a conflict that Canadians cannot at this time really comprehend, and certainly one they cannot afford to have in these times of confusion, of suspicion of government. Individual Canadians do not know what the people next door are going to do or what we are going to do. I think it is our fault that this is an emotional issue, not just the fault of members sitting in the Chamber now but those who have sat here over the last 10, 12, 15 years.
Individual members have talked to the public on this capital punishment proposal and asked them what they want. I assume, Mr. Speaker, as does every member of this House, that the people of Canada have elected us. But what have we done, and why is there suspicion of government in this great country of ours? There is suspicion of government not just federally but provincially too, and as an ex-municipal politician I say even municipally. I see a period of frustration in Canada because the people have lost faith in their politicians. Why have they lost faith, Mr. Speaker? I would think the reason is because of our outlook on life and on Canada. We told the people-this government is at fault, there is no question of that-back
Capital Punishment
in 1967, 1968 or 1969 that capital punishment was still in effect but that the cabinet and government supporters in the back benches were not going to accept it. We have taken the trust of the people of Canada and completely ignored it.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, I am not a long-winded politician, but I should like to comment on a few areas. I like to get at the facts and to hit the people right between the eyes. I would question some of the comments made by the abolitionists. It is not that their views are not legitimate; they feel in their hearts that there should not be capital punishment. But I am sure that many members who agree with the retentionist view, as I do, are getting a little sick and tired of hearing from their colleagues on both sides of the House "You are a hanger"; or, "You believe in capital punishment, you just want to get rid of the problem". That is not the way I feel, and it is not the way my constituents feel in Middlesex-London-Lambton.

Mr. Speaker, I apologize to the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia). I think perhaps it was the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Andres). My concern with that outlook of people who feel that the retentionist attitude is that which I mentioned previously, that is, that we are some sort of monsters who would take somebody who has committed a very heinous crime and demolish them, is that it is not a true outlook. The people who believe in capital punishment are the butcher, the baker, the candlestick maker, the MP, and also the people of Canada who have elected all of us.
We have reached the position now where we say this is not an emotional viewpoint. Some areas have been referred to as emotionalism. I should like to quote from the Dalhou-sie Review, which I understand is the bible of many lawyers in this House. It states:
Sentimentality in the matter of crime and criminals, in which little or no account is taken of any distinction between the new offender and the confirmed outlaw, is perhaps an indication of an overwhelming moral upheaval. Unfortunately, there is no evidence that this genial spirit of "live and let live" and of co-existence with known criminals has resulted in any greater measure of public safety. Quite the contrary. The insecurity of our cities increases year by year as the crime rate in virtually all categories surges relentlessly upward.
What this particular gentleman is saying is that because of our permissiveness, and because of our foregoing of our knowledge of the past, we are ignoring what is happening in Canada today. I agree with him when he suggests to us that we should look into our own hearts first before we prejudge. This is something we have not been doing. We have gone along with snowballing permissiveness, and the attitude of "let them get away with it". Each individual has done the same thing in his own business or his own

area of endeavour. We have taken this attitude and winked at it. This is where that attitude leads us to.
Let me comment very briefly on the presentations the police have made to all members of parliament. My great concern is not in respect of the calibre of police we have today, and not in respect of justice that is presented to us by them under very difficult circumstances. It is very difficult for a policeman to take somebody into court at 8.30 in the morning and see them walk out on the street at 10.30. Policemen exist in their jobs to protect you and me, and all citizens of Canada. They have an obligation to society which perhaps parliamentarians, politicians, and the people have not recognized. They are the people who protect us.
My concern is not in respect of the degree of protection we have received or the diligence with which policemen have performed their duties. My concern rather is in respect of what have we done to them. We have told them there will be no capital punishment for murderers of policemen and prison guards.
Let us assume that this legislation is passed and we do not have capital punishment. Under those circumstances if a criminal comes out of a bank with a gun, will the policeman with the knowledge that no matter what happens to him or what has happened to the poor teller in the bank not be inclined to shoot first to kill? Will he hesitate because of the risk of being down graded? I suggest absolutely not because he is going to be applauded. This is a sad situation. My great concern really is that the police know the background and say. "To hell with it. We cannot depend on the Government of Canada and we cannot depend on the provincial or municipal governments. We will shoot first and ask questions afterwards." I suggest, Mr. Speaker, and members of this august body, that this type of mentality is not that far away.
I have spoken to policemen who have said to me "Larry, will you get some sense into them because we are ready to give up the whole thing." We are getting into a police state where the policemen shoot first. We are losing all sense of justice and fair play, no matter what the circumstances. This concerns me because policemen are the people who are supposed to protect us.
We have heard many statistics on both sides of the question. I will not go into gory details of murder, rape, and such things, and I will not go into detail regarding the contempt we have for murderers or the concern we have for our children. I would like to say this to you in an unemotional way. This is a decision to be made by every member of parliament after serious consideration for some period of time. Many of us have known since 1974 that we were going to have this debate and would have to make this decision. I am sure there is not a member here who will make the decision on any other basis than on the basis of his own feelings and the direction he has received from his constituents. Let us not forget the wishes of our constituents, as they are the ones who have put us here.
In closing I should like to paraphrase Rabbi Plaut, It so happens that my makeup and experience place me and the majority of my constituents, over 75 per cent, on the side of retention. But, having said that, I cannot possibly claim that this makes me right.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on this bill because I doubt whether any other single issue has so plagued and tormented the consciences of Canadians than the case for capital punishment.
There have been some very interesting addresses made on this particular legislation, and I refer here to the speech made tonight by the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle), the speech we just listened to by the hon. member for Middlesex-London-Lambton (Mr. Condon), the one made last evening by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt), and the speech of the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander). Those speakers arrived at different conclusions, but I submit that their thoughts given to this House could not help but make all of us think about the issue.
The doctrine of the sanctity of human life was developed a long time ago and not, it should be noted, by the present Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand). Although compassion for human life is a basic tenet of western civilization, at the beginning of the 19th century in England more than 100 offences were punishable by death. Since then, numerous clergymen, lawyers, sociologists and others have agitated for a humanization of the penal administration. Their efforts succeeded in making our legal system more humane and more just, but in recent years we have, I believe, gone too far. Punishment and retribution have come to be considered unenlightened, and persons advocating them are often condemned as barbarians.
Present thinking, at least that of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the present government, appears to have been influenced by social scientists and criminologists who emphasize social engineering and social justice in order to achieve reform and rehabilitation. I say to you, Sir, that a battered, distraught, dismayed, and concerned society has discovered that these abstract theories linking crime to environmental causes do not translate into concrete programs to protect citizens against violent crime.
To consider specifically capital punishment, I submit that two distinct questions present themselves for examination. First, is the death penalty an effective deterrent to crime? Second, can the taking of a life by the state be justified on moral grounds?
Let us examine the question of deterrence. This matter has been studied at great length, and the Solicitor General's department has engaged various experts who claim to have proven that capital punishment is no more effective a deterrent than a lengthy jail sentence. Before accepting such conclusions I must point out that their whole approach misses the point.
Repayment and retribution, including capital punishment, are important threads in the social fabric, not only because they deter or reform the offender but because they reassure and satisfy society. This is not the satisfaction of some dark animal need. Citizens live in society on the understanding that their lives, their dignity, and their right to enjoy their possessions will be protected. When adequate retribution follows injury, citizens can be reassured and satisfied that society really does place some
May 11, 1976

value on their persons. This, I submit, Mr. Speaker, was, and is, a central need for any society.
From 1961 to 1968, 28 individuals serving death-commuted sentences were paroled after spending an average of, was it 30 years-no, Mr. Speaker; was it 20 years-no, Mr. Speaker. It was after an average of only 12 years in prison prior to release, according to the Department of the Solicitor General in the document entitled "The prevention and control of violent crime in Canada" of March 1975, page 9. From 1968 to 1974 this figure rose to an average of 13.3 years for the 42 persons paroled from death-commuted sentences. In the light of these figures-and these are all the figures I intend to place on the record-it can be seen that the difference between the penalty for armed robbery, and murder, might be only a year or two-and under these circumstances a "death" sentence is hardly a deterrent.
One does not require a Ph.D. in sociology to know that a person who murders in the heat of the moment will not be deterred by the threat of capital punishment. The Criminal Code already allows society to distinguish between capital and non-capital murder. But how can the Solicitor General maintain that total abolition of capital punishment would not make criminals more disposed to killing policemen? This is the point that was just raised by the hon. member for Middlesex-London-Lambton (Mr. Condon). Anyone who thinks criminals do not weigh the possibilities of getting caught, and do not understand they could be executed, is living in a dream world.
A society in which crime goes without real punishment, and in which victims receive no satisfaction for their injury, is one that may turn to vigilante justice. Cynicism and callous indifference to good and evil will result from our having less concern for the needs of those who observe the rules than for those who break them. Regardless of whether punishment deters or rehabilitates, it is necessary for justice. Justice is as much a part of the human condition as is mercy. Without either, society will degenerate into a dispassionate paradise, where there would be neither love nor hate, justice nor mercy, only preventive regulations.
Let us look, for example, at the question of morality. Sooner or later the opponents of capital punishment fall back upon the thesis that the state is altogether without the moral right to assume a prerogative that is God's alone. Admittedly, the deliberate and ceremonial taking of the life of a human being is offensive to most persons and this is why executions, when they do take place, are no longer performed in public.
It is generally agreed that it is wrong for the state to inflict torture, or any hideous punishment, no matter how callous the offence. No less reprehensible is the infliction of death for such offences as theft, embezzlement, smuggling, bribery, counterfeiting, or seditious utterances. Yet in protest against such inhumanity, should we unthinkingly jump to the opposite extreme and claim that no crime, however, dastardly, is deserving of the death penalty? These are the questions we must ask ourselves.
The right of an individual to take the life of another in defence of his person is hardly contested. Why is it proper on occasion for a private citizen to take the life of another, while the state may not do so under any circumstances whatsoever? Again, if it is allowable to deprive a would-be
Capital Punishment
murderer of his life in order to forestall a crime, why does it become morally reprehensible to do so after the crime has been committed?
It will be argued, no doubt, that an act of murder, once having been comrrytted, is irreversible. And since nothing can be done to restore the victim to life, hanging the murderer becomes no more than a wanton act of vengeance. But it should be noted that the renunciation of vengeance is a virtue far more easily exercised by the dispassionate onlooker at a crime than by the sorrowing relatives who are directly afflicted.
It is also frequently argued that a man who has been hanged for murder might, on later verification, be proven guiltless. It is a historical fact that in every country, and in every age, innocent persons have been harried to their doom through the machinations of private enemies as well as by hatreds begotten of religion and politics. Such scandals cannot be entirely ruled out for the future; but they can be counteracted to some extent by modern criminal procedures now in force which provide almost iron-clad guarantees to an accused person. He is safeguarded by stringent laws of evidence, and he is seldom lacking in experienced counsel. Invariably a verdict of murder is subject to minute scrutiny through a series of appeals and reviews.
It is true that a vast number of prosecutions do leave behind them a strong element of doubt. Indeed, a trial is meant, by its very nature, to distinguish between that which is certain and that which remains unconvincing. In a great number of acquittals, the accused is discharged, not after being certified innocent and harmless, but only because the charge against him has not been proved beyond all reasonable doubt. In cases where any doubt remains, it is always the accused who is entitled to benefit. But it must also be acknowledged that not all court proceedings necessarily leave a residue of doubt. Often the charge against the accused is easily substantiated, the testimony of the prosecution's witnesses fully corroborated, and all contradictory evidence conspicuous by its total absence.
There is not a single human enterprise or field of activity not marred by some regrettable episodes. Yet we do not prohibit the construction of tall buildings or bridges, or tunnels because it is possible some two or three persons might lose their lives in the course of such an operation. Acts of justice, designed as effectively as possible to protect the innocent, will unquestionably be accompanied now and again by tragic blunders. But unless such miscarriages become blatant, and of alarming extent, there is nothing to be done except to minimize them as far as is humanly possible. In any event, such errors, tragic though they must be, could at their worst be insignificant, as compared with opposite blunders in which further loss of innocent lives could be the direct consequence of thoughtless clemency extended to dangerous and unrepentant assassins. I can therefore come to only one conclusion.
Capital punishment can be defended on both moral and practical grounds. However, for the death penalty to play any significant role in the war against crime it must be enforced not only at rare intervals but in all cases of fully

May 11, 1976
Capital Punishment
proven capital murder. What matters almost as much as the severity of punishment is its certainty. Since 1967, 33 policemen and two prison guards have been slain, but the cabinet has continually overruled the findings of the judges, juries, and even the law itself, most recently in the case of Gary John McNamara who murdered a prison guard in 1972. On May 9, 1974, the cabinet commuted the sentence but no reason was given.
In 1973 Rene Vaillancourt murdered a Toronto policeman while fleeing the scene of a bank hold-up. In 1974 James Hutchinson and Richard Ambrose killed two officers in Moncton. Less than four months ago a policeman and a taxi driver were killed in Dartmouth. It is quite clear from statements made by the Solicitor General that the cabinet has no intention of allowing capital punishment in any of these cases. If that is to be the case, at least parliament should consider amending the Criminal Code so that murderers of policemen and prison guards have to spend the rest of their lives in jail, and are not out walking the streets again in 12 years or less.
Many Canadians suspect that the actual time served already for violent crimes may be too light. A combination of factors account for some relatively short prison terms now: at the court room level many murder charges get reduced to manslaughter because it is claimed some unpleasant remark made by the victim provoked the murderer. Provocation reduces murder to manslaughter, and this defence is helped by the convenience of not having the victim around to testify. Manslaughter sentences may put offenders back on the streets fairly fast. In 1973 almost 83 per cent of the sentences given for murder-reduced-to-manslaughter were under ten years. Over half of those were under five years, which could mean parole in 18 months, or day parole much earlier.
Of 27 murderers discharged from prison in 1973-actually 37 were discharged but statistics are available on only 27-five served less than four years and 21 served between five and nine years. Of manslaughter discharges, 67 per cent had served less than three years. Of attempted murder discharges, 77 per cent had served less than four years. In rape convictions-an offence for which only the most brutal attackers generally get to court-94 per cent of those released had served less than three years. Given these statistics, Canadians may well be excused for thinking that the length of incarceration is more often than not grotesquely out of proportion to all the havoc, pain, torment, and misery created by the criminal.
One of the most thought provoking editorials on this thorny problem appeared on February 28 in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, and I want to put it on the record in the time allowed me this evening because I think it sums up the views of the majority of Nova Scotians. It is entitled, "The Death Penalty", and it read as follows:
There is little doubt but that the majority of Canadian people wish to retain the death penalty, at least for some types of murder.
Government, in most of its programs, cites the pressure of public opinion and the necessity to respond to that opinion as justification.
In the instance of the death penalty, government is careful not to cite public opinion which is adverse to the chosen course.
Of recent years there has grown up a theory, on which much policy has been based, that the rights of the criminal are more important than the rights of society.

In turn that has brought about a backlash in the public which is increasingly concerned with the protection of persons and property, the administration of justice has frequently appeared to concentrate largely upon issues of conceding to the demands and requirements of the criminal element with little thought of fundamental rights of law-abiding citizens.
For practical purposes the death sentence in Canada, while technically in effect, has been suspended. The result of that suspension has not been a decline in violent crime.
I am going to repeat that paragraph:
For practical purposes the death sentence in Canada, while technically in effect, has been suspended. The result of that suspension has not been a decline in violent crime.
The criminal who deliberately plans and executes a murder has no concern with the life of the victim. Yet that same criminal immediately demands and receives the full protection of society when apprehended. And that same criminal along with those who advocate his cause, will present a long list of reasons why his life ought not be forfeited.
The dispassionate killer will not reform. And the program now proposed by government will be of no help.
What is planned is to put people who are proven menaces to society away for a stipulated 25 years. For practical purposes that is life and the form and nature of the sentence is a guarantee of increasing the dangers to custodial staff and the complexities of control.
In proposing its alternative to the death sentence the government is suggesting that the Canadian people get the worst of both worlds. They will pay higher costs with no assurance of improved safety for society.
The death penalty represents the final right of organized society to rid itself of those who will not conform in any respect to civilized life. Such people are a minority, and are not to be confused with others who may take life in passion.
Removal of the final right of society, in effect, tells the criminal that however vicious and evil the crime his own life will not be threatened, but rather will be protected by the society for which he has himself shown no mercy .. .
Parliament is intended to reflect the wishes of the people of Canada.
I am going to read that slowly because I want as many hon. members as are in the Chamber to hear these words.
Parliament is intended to reflect the wishes of the people of Canada.
Surely that is why we are here.

The institution has been down-graded of recent years, not always with the most constructive of consequences.
The use of power, simply because power is held, to thwart the public will is an assurance of a further erosion among the populace of confidence in not only the government, but parliament itself.
In recent years it has often appeared that the majority has no rights. Since we last debated the issue in January of 1973 I submit that the cabinet and the government have, by their actions, undermined our legal processes. They have undermined the power of parliament. The practice that has been followed has in effect removed any deterrent associated
May 11, 1976

with the death penalty. This government in more ways than one has made a sham of our whole judicial process.
How can we expect society to have any respect for the law when those who are supposed to uphold it make a mockery of its own rules and regulations? These actions can no longer be tolerated. I believe we must set an example for the entire country if parliament is to remain supreme. In my opinion, anyone who accidentally kills another during a fight or in the heat of an argument should not be hanged but should be given life imprisonment. However, I believe that capital punishment should be retained for all those convicted of planned, premeditated murder. Clemency, which is the prerogative of the Crown, should be granted only when mercy has been recommended by the jury at the trial, or in the case of an established error in conviction.
I agree that the rights of a murderer as an individual must be protected, but I ask you, Sir, is it not way past the time when we should be considering the rights of the victim?
I had an opportunity to speak on this subject when it was last before the House, and when it was before the House prior to that, but tonight I want to quote just one paragraph from my own words as put on the record on January 31, 1973, when I said the following:
No matter how we vote in this House on this issue, it is my firm conviction that we shall never again see a man hanged in Canada or put to death by any other means. I say this in light of the facts, for the federal cabinet has exercised its so-called executive prerogative of mercy more than 60 times during the past ten years by commuting all death sentences meted out by the courts.
Of course these figures are updated by what I have put on the record tonight.
In conclusion, I must say to this House that until a suitable alternative to capital punishment is proposed as a protection for society, I feel that the government has left me no choice but to vote against this bill.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to enter this debate because it is the most sensitive issue I have to face as a new member of parliament representing my constituency. Other more senior members in this Chamber have dealt with this issue before, and I have found them to be of considerable help and guidance to me, whether they be for or against. Before stating my proposition with respect to this matter, there is one issue I wish to deal with, namely, the free vote.
A free vote to me means just that-a vote based on one's own conscience, but it also means one which should at least take into account the representations of my constituents. In other words, I do not think that I have the right on such a sensitive issue as capital punishment to be blind to the feelings of my constituents. The cynicism I have heard from some hon. members in the media regarding the decision by the government to allow a free vote shocks me, to say the least. As a backbencher on this side of the House I want to put on the record that the whips have not been placed on me to vote the way the cabinet intends to vote. I respect their collective decision, and I know that they respect others who have opposite views.
Capital Punishment
I would now like to deal with the substance of the issue. The government has introduced a bill to abolish the death penalty for murder and to replace capital punishment with life sentences. First degree murderers would not normally be eligible for parole until they have served a minimum of 25 years.
My personal feelings on the issue of the death penalty, I believe, are not the important question in deciding how I vote. What is most important is the need to provide society and the law abiding individual with a sense of protection from those who commit the ultimate act of violence against the person. Society does have a right to protect itself from those who prey upon its citizens. I believe the death penalty can act as a deterrent to premeditated murder, and I intend to vote for the retention of capital punishment for premeditated murder regardless of who the victim is.
For non-premeditated murders, I believe that the minimum sentence without parole, such as the 10 year non-parolable period proposed for second degree murder in the government's bill, is a sufficient deterrent.
I have made a distinction between premeditated and unpremeditated murder. Such a distinction is not one solely based on the legal definition of planned and deliberate murder, but premeditation must be considered to be a question of fact and personal judgment. I have faith in our trial and jury system that such a distinction can be made in each case. After hearing all the evidence, a jury under the guidance of a trial judge can distinguish between, to use the extremes, the contract killing and the murder which results from a domestic quarrel, or to put it another way, murder which results from a fit of passion.
This to me is the beauty and justice of our legal system: the inherent right of every accused to be tried as an individual, taking into account the facts of the case as determined by a jury, under the guidance of a trial judge as to the questions of law.
With respect to the matter of deterrence, I at one time thought that capital punishment was not a deterrent, but I am convinced now that it is. I have read most of the technical reports, including Fattah's, regarding this particular matter. They leave me with the conclusion that capital punishment may not be a deterrent. I stress the word "may". That word to me . expresses a probability. Accordingly, if there is even the remotest chance that capital punishment may prevent a murder, how can I deny that victim, whoever it will be, that possibility of prevention? It is the matter of prevention of death that I am concerned with, not revenge. Society does have the right to protect itself from its most despicable crime against its citizens.
I would now like to deal with the matter of long sentences as proposed by Bill C-84. As I understand it, Bill C-84 intends to break murder into two degrees, first and second degree, both of which will carry life imprisonment but with different minimum periods that must be served in a penitentiary before the convicted person will be eligible for parole consideration. The penalty for second degree murder will basically stay the same, but with respect to first degree murder the new legislation provides for a penalty of life imprisonment with an absolute term of imprisonment of 25 years with no parole. I fully realize and

May 11, 1976
Capital Punishment
appreciate that there is a provision for judicial review of either penalties by a panel of three superior court justices.
Solely as it relates to the proposed offence of first degree murder, I seriously question the incarceration of an individual for such a great length of time, notwithstanding the review provisions. Are we not doing that individual more harm than good? I do not know the definitive answer to that question, and none of the technical reports that I have read have given me the answer. In fact, the Solicitor General's own department in a publication entitled, "Questions and Answers Relating to the Capital Punishment Issue" states as follows:
question: If long sentences replace capital punishment, what implications does this have for increasing the incidence of suicide, mental illness and hostility among persons convicted of murder?
RESPONSE: Behavioural scientists have noted neurotic and psychotic reactions associated with long term institutionalization. However, this is based upon clinical experience from which it is sometimes difficult to establish if it is actually the institutionalization which is the cause. Also, there is little scientific documentation available as to whether or not suicide and hostility among persons serving long term sentences is associated with long term incarceration. Since there are many interrelated factors, it is impossible to predict what effects the proposed legislation will have upon suicide, mental illness, and hostility within Canadian institutions.
The answer acknowledges that experts do not know the effect of incarceration of an individual for a long term. The recent examples at the B.C. Penitentiary in my province may be extremes, to say the least, but they may well indicate the results of either deplorable conditions, or long term incarceration, or a combination of both. If one were to lock one up in the penthouse of a luxury hotel for a minimum of 25 years, I am sure that such incarceration would have some psychological effect on the individual. The point is, Mr. Speaker, that a prison is a prison whether it be the British Columbia penitentiary or, as I have exaggerated, the penthouse of a luxury hotel. Certainly I agree with the reforms that we have made in penal institutions and I earnestly hope that we will continue to do so, but whatever we do, we must remember that a prison is still a prison.
But, more important, with respect to long term incarceration, B.C. Police Commission Chairman, Dr. John Hogarth, has called the sentencing provisions "overly rigid" and said it would be dangerous to deprive prisoners of any hope of eventual release. In essence, I think he is saying, and I agree, that what Bill C-84 does is symbolically kill an individual by subjecting him to sometimes very cruel circumstances for 25 years. I want to know, and I know my constituents want to know, whether long term incarceration increases the potential for attack on prison guards and policemen. From my discussions with some of the officials of correctional institutions in the Pacific region where the B.C. Penitentiary is located, I know that the staff-guards for example-are extremely uneasy about the prospects of long term incarceration.
Notwithstanding the fact that Section 674 of the proposed legislation would deal with the abhorrent situation of a murderer under parole, including day pass or temporary pass, committing another murder, I find that Section 674 enshrines the inescapable conclusions that this legislation is symbolic killing. At present, as I understand it, a

person whose sentence is commuted must serve a minimum of ten years before he becomes eligible for parole; and this period could be extended but for no more than 20 years. Section 674 as proposed states:
(1)	Unless the Parliament of Canada otherwise provides by an enactment making express reference to this section, no person who has been sentenced to imprisonment for life without eligibility for parole for a specified number of years pursuant to this act shall be considered for parole or released pursuant to the terms of a grant of parole under the Parole Act or any other act of the Parliament of Canada until the expiration or termination of his specified number of years of imprisonment without eligibility for parole.
(2)	Notwithstanding the Penitentiary Act and the Parole Act, in the case of any person sentenced to imprisonment for life without eligibility for parole for a specified number of years pursuant to this act, no absence without escort may be authorized under the Penitentiary Act and no day parole may be granted under the Parole Act until the expiration of all but three years of his number of years of imprisonment without eligibility for parole.
In other words, a person convicted of first degree murder would have to serve 22 years of his sentence before being eligible for day parole or a temporary pass.
Again I reiterate and submit that this legislation is nothing more than symbolic killing. I earnestly hope that the hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) will answer some of the questions I have raised on the issue of long term incarceration.
Before concluding, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that I am in full agreement with those who state that capital punishment will not prove to be a cure-all to all our criminal problems. The issue of crime in a pluristic and democratic society is much too complex and intricate for anybody to be so simplistic as to suggest the answer lies in, "Hang them all", to use the current expression. We must attack some of the more fundamental roots of crime, for example, poverty.
Other measures that the government has introduced, such as Bill C-71, particularly as it relates to the tightening of our bail law, and at present Bill C-83, particularly as it relates to gun control legislation, dangerous offenders, and wiretap provisions, are steps in the right direction. The criminal law, like any other law, is and should be a process of constant review and amendment by this and future parliaments. Having said that, I still maintain that society must have the right to protect itself from those who prey upon it.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the advanced hour I shall give a short preamble to the speech I intend to make in this debate.
The question which should concern us during this debate, and which has not been examined by any of my colleagues so far, is not whether we should retain or abolish capital punishment, but rather whether or not we should reintroduce some form of capital punishment.
My reasoning, Mr. Speaker, is very simple. The Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) has repeatedly stated that he will not sign an execution order as long as he is in office. In response to my colleague from the Yukon on the night of the opening of this debate, he shouted across the emotionally charged expanse of this Chamber, "If you want to hang someone, get yourself another boy." Since our con-

stituents, who expect to have their majority view represented in parliament, only change their "boys" during elections, the question of the abolition or retention of capital punishment is irrelevant until about 1978.
As a matter of fact, the "if or not" has not been an issue since 1963, even though the question has been debated in the House four times since then. The question which will be put to the members at the end of this debate will only decide, therefore, whether capital punishment will be abolished with the consent of parliament and the Canadian people, or by the continued abuse of the royal or executive prerogative.
