subtopic: SPORTS-REASON FOR ALLEGED DOUBLE STANDARD IN DEALING WITH SOUTH AFRICA
SPORTS-REASON FOR ALLEGED DOUBLE STANDARD IN DEALING WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the reason I am taking part in the adjournment debate once again is because there seems to be a concern which relates to the fact that the government is once again exemplifying inconsistencies in regard to its policies, this time by taking a hypocritically double standard position relating to its involvement with South Africa.
I am specifically referring to the obviously abrupt attitude the Department of National Health and Welfare has taken in respect of the 1976 Olympiad for the Physically Disabled, scheduled to be held in Etobicoke later this summer. These very prestigious and worth-while games for disabled athletes from around the world are traditionally held every four years in the country hosting the regular Olympic games, while in subsequent years they are held at Stokes Manderville, England.
Canadian organizers and department officials must have known for years that these games would be held in Canada in 1976 in conjunction with the regular Olympic games, which will be held in Montreal this summer as well. These same officials must have known for just as many years that included in the games would be a team representing South Africa. These two facts are common knowledge- common knowledge, as precedence alone would show, to those who are in touch with reality as it relates to sport. Certainly the minister and his department should be in touch with what goes on in the sports world as such matters fall under his jurisdiction.
Adjournment Debate
My point is, that the government had promised a $500,000 grant to the organizers of the Olympiad in Etobicoke, with the knowledge that a team from South Africa would be represented. I say this since in several previous Olympiads for the disabled a South African team did take part, with Canadian teams competing as well in some games.
After preparations were well under way the department suddenly decided to withhold aid, the aid having been promised on the condition that South Africans would not attend, or withdraw.
The irony of the double standard is twofold. First, on at least two previous occasions, once in 1972, for the Munich Games and again last year in England, this government, under the auspices of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) funded Canadian teams for the purpose of participating with South African teams. Incidentally, South Africa at that time had not taken steps to eliminate racial discrimination. The government now is withholding promised funds on grounds of racial discrimination, even though on two previous occasions the government had provided funds. Since then the South African team has officially joined the International Sports Organization for the Disabled and, at the same time, officially amended its constitution to prohibit racial or political discrimination. This is proven by the fact thkt a team of 22 athletes scheduled to compete in Etobicoke this summer includes 9 non-whites and blacks.
That is not all, Mr. Speaker. When questioned, the Minister of National Health and Welfare stated that the government's policy has been very clearly established for many years regarding the apartheid policy in South Africa, and the government's position has been to withhold its financial aid to sporting events involving South Africa because of its apartheid policy. The question one must ask oneself, indeed I am asking it, is this: if this in fact is the policy of the federal government, why did it fund the Canadian teams previously when that policy was in force? Second and more important, if indeed this is the policy of the federal government, why has the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce opened at least two offices in South Africa, with the intention of opening more locations for the purpose of expanding trade between our two states?
I have nothing against the government using South Africa as a trading partner and thereby recognizing that state, but why the double standard? Why take it out on sports? Why involve politics with sports? More specifically, why take it out on disabled kids? That, to me, is petty.
The government tells Canadian athletes and organizations it will not fund them if they invite South Africans; at the same time it allowed Canadian businessmen to import approximately $180 million worth of South African goods last year, mainly wines, sugar, and other products. In addition the government exerted no pressure to stop the massive campaign advertising South African wine for sale in Canada. Nobody has complained about this. But it shows that there is a double standard. This inconsistency concerns me and many others who are involved in these worthwhile games. By picking on the disabled the government is being small, petty, and hypocritical, to say the least. Once again thanks goes to this two-faced government

May 11, 1976
Adjournment Debate
for jeopardizing the dreams and hopes of nearly 2,000 wheelchair, blind, and amputee athletes from around the world.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: SPORTS-REASON FOR ALLEGED DOUBLE STANDARD IN DEALING WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have only three minutes to answer the small, petty, and hypocritical statement made by the hon. member opposite. I remind him that despite the apparent change of policy referred to in a specific case, apartheid is no less rigorously enforced in athletic competition than in any other sphere of South African life.
It is worth noting that in 1970 the International Olympic Committee suspended South Africa completely from participating in the Olympic movement. This position was given unqualified support by the United Nations, and it is supported fully by the government. We fully support the Olympiad in Etobicoke and have given our enthusiastic and full support right from the beginning; but the organizers of that competition knew in the early stages of the organization of this competition the position of the Canadian government vis-a-vis participation by South African athletes in any such competition.
The Canadian government policy denies funding to any Canadian athlete or group of athletes who intend to travel to South Africa to participate in an athletic competition. While we fully recognize that the decision to participate or not rests with the individual and/or sports body concerned, we have pointed out that competition in South African under conditions of racial discrimination, which are universally condemned, is a matter of considerable concern. Although the government does not financially support such visits, neither is it prepared to limit the freedom of Canadians to travel abroad where they wish.
More recently, events have been awarded to Canada in which athletes from South Africa have been invited to participate. I wish to confirm the position taken by the government in July of 1975 of not providing either moral or financial support to any event in Canada to which South African athletes have been invited. This policy is being implemented in concert with many other nations, in the hope that concern over increasing isolation will encourage the South African government to take real and substantive steps to abandon the policy and practice of apartheid.
Recently representations have been made to the government concerning the staging in Canada of the Olympiad for the Physically Disabled, requesting that the government policy be modified for the Olympiad. It was the view of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Mac-Eachen) and myself that such a modification was not justified. The government has reviewed on a continuing basis reports from our mission in South Africa on apar-thied in sports. We do not believe that circumstances in this country have changed materially, even though the South African government may allow modification in a particular case. This view has been confirmed in recent days by the reaffirmation by the Supreme Council of Sport in Africa of its continued opposition to all sports contacts with the regime in South Africa. I can only feel sorry that some people resort to using handicapped people in this particular situation.

subtopic: HEALTH-MEASURES TO PROTECT VISITORS TO OLYMPIC GAMES AGAINST POLIO-POSSIBLE USE OF SABIN ORAL VACCINE
HEALTH-MEASURES TO PROTECT VISITORS TO OLYMPIC GAMES AGAINST POLIO-POSSIBLE USE OF SABIN ORAL VACCINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to see the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) in the Chamber this evening. It is very considerate of him to be here to give us the benefit of his advice.
According to reports the minister stated, "Don't push the panic button on polio viruses." Certainly the carrying out of corrective measures should not be carried out in panic. However, perhaps the polio viruses found in the sewage draining into the Ottawa River has awakened the department's concern out of its Ferdinand slumbers.
It is interesting that I, a member of this House, was denied any information from the department without going through the Director of Public Relation for the department. He could not be reached. I am sure the minister will have an answer for us and say that he had nothing to do with this. The minister knows that I have never misused information given to me by any department. I only wanted this information to correlate my address tonight.
There appears to be a considerable number of people in the province of Ontario who are not immune or who have no antibody immunity to poliomyelitis. This may also be the case in other provinces. I am concerned because through two polio epidemics I was the Medical Officer of Health for the province in the days before polio vaccine. Anyone who has been through such an epidemic, and who has seen those cases and the number who died or were left crippled, would be concerned with the present attitude. I recall pregnant young mothers, young men, and children who died. In particular I remember two young ladies who went swimming together, contracted the disease and died. I will not elaborate on this, but I wonder how many of the present generation have forgotten the days before Salk vaccine.
I am concerned that every step be taken to ensure that those who have not been immunized will be before attending the Olympic Games. In the schools this program will have to be initiated right away before the school term ends to get the school-agers vaccinated and to set up clinics if found necessary.
I am interested and concerned because of a survey done in 1969 by medical officers of health of 15 areas, one of which was the city of Barrie in the riding of Simcoe North. Blood samples were collected in the schools by teams from the Connaught Laboratories. In each area samples were taken from 175 people in four age groups: pre-school children age four to six years; from parents, in most cases the mothers who accompanied the children, ages 23 to 45 years; children in grades seven to eight, ages 11-13; and young people in the age group 15 to 17 years. Immunization cards for each school age child were obtained from health unit records. Blood samples from .3 to .5 millilitres were obtained by finger puncture and collected in blood collecting tubes. This was tested in cultures of monkey kidney cells for antibodies of each of the three types of polio virus.
May 11, 1976

For children 11 to 13 and 15 to 17, there was a high percentage of resistance to the disease. In the age group 4-6 years, the percentage was less. It was found that only 65 per cent of the children four to six years had antibodies to all three types of polio virus-antibodies being due almost entirely to the Salk vaccine. In the children who had received six or more doses, 74 per cent had antibodies to the three types. In ages 11 to 13 and 15 to 17, there was a high percentage with antibodies to polio virus. This was accounted for by the fact that these children had not only the Salk vaccine but were given the Sabin vaccine in the mass campaign of 1962. Also, some may have shown immunity through having had a previous low grade infection.
It is interesting to note that of those who had not been immunized, three out of six aged 11 to 13 years, and five out of seven in ages 15 to 17, had antibodies to all three types of polio.
From all I can learn it would appear that one dose of Sabin vaccine following immunization with Salk vaccine seems to give full protection against polio virus. It is also true that over the years there has been some increase in the Salk vaccine particularly in type 3 antigen which stimulates the production of antibodies. The type 2 antigen was decreased early in 1974.
The Salk vaccine will stop the neuromuscular effects of polio in practically all cases but does not always stop the gastroenteritis or pharyngitis which may follow particularly the wild viruses.
The disturbing question and one which must be answered is whether immunization has been sufficient to ensure safe immunity to polio. When you look at the age group four to six and see that only 65 per cent had immunity, it would indicate that this is not adequate protection. Again the question is raised that those in the 11 to 13 and 15 to 17 age group had higher immunity due to the fact that they may have had a previous sub-clinical infection and that they also had Sabin vaccine along with the Salk vaccine. Antibodies in those four to six were almost entirely due to immunization with Salk vaccine.
It would appear that there must be a drive put on to encourage immunization. I would suggest that the minister, in his capacity as senior minister of health in Canada, urge that a full immunization program be started without delay. Then, and only then, can we be assured that we have done what we should do with the knowledge we have of the viruses of polio, which it appears at the moment require further study, and regarding which a further report will be out next week. I also want to draw to the minister's attention that, as far as I know, all provinces, with the exception of Ontario and Nova Scotia, use the Sabin vaccine.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-MINING NICKEL FROM SEABED-INVOLVEMENT OF WORKERS IN DEVELOPING STRATEGY FOR NEGOTIATIONS POSITION TAKEN BY INCO
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-MINING NICKEL FROM SEABED-INVOLVEMENT OF WORKERS IN DEVELOPING STRATEGY FOR NEGOTIATIONS POSITION TAKEN BY INCO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the nickel industry in Canada may very shortly be facing a serious crisis which can only spell disaster for those communities and workers who are very dependent on this particular mineral.
At the recent Law of the Sea Conference the United States, our major trading partner, presented plans which if carried out will, over a period of ten to 25 years, mean the extinction of nickel mining in Canada. The plan presented by the United States calls for the mining of nickel resources from the seabed beyond the 200-mile limit, thus effectively placing the industry beyond the jurisdiction of nations or of trade unions. They want the amount of this seabed mining to increase by a minimum of 6 per cent a year, in spite of the fact that demand will not increase that quickly.
Present increases in nickel output are shared among the world's nickel producing countries. Canada, in fact, used to supply over 50 per cent of the world's nickel requirements, but its share of the market has been dropping to the point where Canada supplies slightly over 30 per cent of the world's nickel needs.
According to Charles Elliot, a director and former president of the Mining Association of Canada, an increase in production of undersea nickel of the magnitude the United States envisages would constitute a disaster for the Canadian nickel mining industry.
When we speak of a disaster to the Canadian nickel mining industry we are not just talking about a drop in profits on shares held by shareholders of the companies. We are talking about the lives of whole communities which

May 11, 1976
Adjournment Debate
are completely dependent on the nickel mining industry. We are talking about the death of such communities as Thompson, Manitoba, and Fort Saskatchewan. We are talking about completely destroying the economic base of the Sudbury Basin, my own riding and yours, Mr. Speaker. In that area alone 13,000 people are employed by INCO and another 4,000 are employed by Falconbridge. Counting the workers' families and all the persons who are involved in the service sector of the Basin's economy we can get the full impact any such cutback would entail.
Just today Statistics Canada revealed that the unemployment rate in this country is 7.4 per cent. If the nickel industry in Canada is wiped out, we can imagine the implication both in human and economic terms for Canada. As developed nations like the United States strive to become self-sufficient in resources, having learned their bitter lesson after the OPEC situation, our pigeons are coming home to roost.
Past actions by provincial and federal governments to allow Canada to develop as a resource economy have left us basically hewers of wood and drawers of water. Lacking the industrial base we need to process our own minerals to finished products, we are now finding ourselves at the mercy of these sorts of changes as proposed by the United States at the Law of the Sea Conference.
While it is very clear that Canadian workers, in fact all Canadians, will be hurt by this kind of action, we can bet our bottom dollars that the nickel mining companies are flexible enough to benefit from the switch from surface mining to undersea mining. As a matter of fact international Nickel Company, Canada's major nickel mining company, is part of the consortium that will be mining the seabed for nickel. Indeed, Mr. Elliot of the Mining Association of Canada made this crystal clear when he said:
The Canadian mining companies and their shareholders might benefit considerably, however, by getting involved in sea bed operations.
So much for the patriotism of big business. Who has the gall to suggest to me the equality of the corporation and the union?
The International Nickel Company Limited, has just changed its name to the International Nickel Company Limited, a move that has some justification considering its probable role in this problem. It is making profits from Canadian workers and Canadian resources now. But if this situation goes the other way and it is decided to mine from the sea, it will make a profit there too. The company has a foot in both camps and you can be sure it will put pressure on all governments concerned to take the steps which will be most profitable to the company. If it turns out to be more profitable to go after the under sea nickel, and this is quite likely considering that the U.S. government is obviously prepared to subsidize these operations with large sums of money, then it will phase out its surface operations.
The Canadian government appears to have been caught with its pants down in the latest revelation by the United States at the Law of the Sea Conference. It is quite obvious that the Americans have already lobbied the other nickel producing countries and promised them a share in any increased production in nickel as a result of seabed mining.
This, of course, leaves Canada on the outside looking in. With friends like that, who needs enemies?
At this moment the Canadian government should be sitting down with those directly affected by this proposal, the workers, the communities, and the mining companies, to determine strategy and plan proposals which would be much fairer to all concerned.
Moreover, the federal government should elicit from International Nickel Company and all other nickel mining companies which may have feet in both camps their full support for the government's position. The government ought to be prepared to nationalize immediately any of those companies which do not support the position which the government puts forward.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Robert Gauthier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-MINING NICKEL FROM SEABED-INVOLVEMENT OF WORKERS IN DEVELOPING STRATEGY FOR NEGOTIATIONS POSITION TAKEN BY INCO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the name of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), I would first express the concern of this government over the nickel proposal tabled at the very end of the last session of the United Nations Conference on the Law of the Sea, which ended on Friday, May 7. That proposal, most likely originating from the United States, is aimed at controlling the production of minerals in the international zone of the sea bed, by restricting it to the annual increase in the world nickel market, arbitrarily estimated at 6 per cent. If adopted, that formula might have serious repercussions on the production of nickel in Canada and other countries, in cases for instance where the actual yearly expansion of the nickel market were below 6 per cent. Canada feels such a formula is unacceptable.
When the Secretary of State for External Affairs met the American Secretary of State, Mr. Kissinger, in Nairobi, he took the opportunity to explain the effect on Canada of such a provision. It was agreed our two countries will hold consultations at the official level to find a solution. Similarly, the American representatives to the Conference on the Law of the Sea implied they had no intention of solving at the expense of Canada the problems faced by the United States in respect of mineral resource supplies.
I should add that, paradoxically, such a controversial formula was never discussed at the Conference on the Law of the Sea. It is however expected it will have high priority on the agenda of the next meeting slated for August. Canada for her part is urging a solution that would protect land producers of nickel, copper, cobalt and manganese, while allowing mining of these minerals from the international sea bed to the benefit of the international community. Our delegation at the conference already expressed these views to other countries that might be affected by the American formula. For the most part, they share our concerns.
We do not yet know INCO's reaction, or that of other mining companies. It would however be quite normal, and even desirable, if representatives of miners' unions, the mining industry and the provinces affected expressed their views to the government before the next meeting to be held in August 1976.
